Well, I've been trying to learn Spanish for a few years now, but it's harder than I thought. I mean, I can understand a lot, but I can't say it properly. It's like I'm trying to speak with a thick accent, and it's so frustrating.      I can imagine. I tried with an app once, and it just drilled me with grammar and vocabulary. It didn’t help me speak at all. I got stuck on the verb conjugations. It’s like trying to learn a new language with a textbook when you're used to speaking.      Exactly! I think I need more practice. I've been watching Spanish TV shows, but I still struggle to follow them. I get the gist, but not the details. What about you? Did you ever try immersion?      Yeah, I did. For a while, I tried to watch Spanish movies with subtitles and even tried speaking with a tutor online. But the tutor didn’t speak fast enough, and I felt embarrassed. I mean, why would I want to practice with someone who speaks slower than me?      Oh, I’ve been there. It’s so hard to ask for help when you're not confident. I remember one time, I got stuck on the word for “tomorrow.” I asked my tutor, and they said, “¿Mañana?” and I thought, “Oh, that’s easy.” But then I realized I’d been saying it wrong for weeks. It was so embarrassing!      That sounds like a classic case of what I call “linguistic guilt.” You feel like you’re failing because you can’t speak as well as you want to. I think the key is to not be too hard on yourself. It’s a process, you know.      You’re right. I think I need to start using a different method. Maybe focusing more on speaking rather than grammar. At first, it was hard, but over time, it started to come naturally. I think the best way is to embrace the struggle. If you’re patient, it’ll happen.      I suppose you’re right. I just need to stop worrying about being perfect. It’s about progress, not perfection. I think I’ll try that—just speaking even if it’s wrong.

So, I just got a text from my cousin, and she’s saying her car’s broken down on the A1 again. I mean, is it always like that? I can imagine. I mean, they’re not all like that, though. I know some people who ride responsibly. But yeah, there’s definitely a whole culture out there that thinks they’re above the law. Well, I think it's time we talk about that tennis thing, Jamie. You've been asking about it more and more lately.      Yeah, Dad, I’m serious about trying again. So, I was just telling my mates about the napkins we had at the family dinner last night. They looked like underpants!      Oh, really? You know, I used to do that with the little ones when they were younger. Got them to think it was a joke. So, I was thinking the other day about what would happen if we had an imaginary party with some of our favorite historical figures. Maybe someone like Frida Kahlo? I might end up using something that’s not in the dictionary, and then I’ll have to explain it to everyone. I’m not sure how that would go over.      You know what? If you use a longer word, it might block their chances of getting a high-scoring move. But I always found that it’s better to be safe than sorry.      That’s true. But I think it’s also about enjoying the game. If you’re playing for fun, then even if you use a strange word, it’s all part of the experience. I always thought it was more about the camaraderie than the score.      I suppose that’s right. I just want to have some fun with it, not stress too much. I’ve been thinking about the other things we talk about on Facebook—like that music magazine we both like. You know, the one that has all these great reviews.      Yes, I’ve been reading that too. I think there’s an article about a new indie band that’s gaining a lot of attention.

Well, I've just been thinking about those days in Germany. I remember the first time I set up an exhibition there. It was in Düsseldorf, I believe. I had this idea to combine traditional printmaking with modern marketing techniques. It was a bit of a gamble, but things took off.      That sounds fascinating. I’ve always been curious about how people make their mark in such a competitive field. What inspired you to start that kind of work?      Oh, it started as a hobby. I was an artist, you see, but I always had a fascination with how art could be more accessible. I used to sell prints at local markets, and then I thought, why not bring that to a wider audience? I realized that if I could market the art effectively, it would reach more people, and that’s when the whole idea of inventing printing systems came about.      That’s a clever approach. I suppose marketing in the arts isn’t as straightforward as in other fields, though. How did you handle the challenge of getting people to engage with your prints?      Well, I started by building a network. I traveled to exhibitions across Germany, met with gallery owners, and even did some workshops. I learned a lot from other artists and marketers. It was a mix of trial and error, but eventually, I developed a system that worked. It wasn’t just about the prints; it was about the experience.      That’s impressive. I always thought that retirement was a time to slow down, but it seems like you found a new purpose. How did you manage to keep it going?      Honestly, it was a passion. I never stopped creating. I had the gallery, so it was an extension of my work. I even started mentoring young artists. It gave me a sense of fulfillment, even if I wasn’t working for a company anymore.      That’s wonderful. I used to work in a similar field, though not as creatively. I suppose we both ended up in a position where we could explore our own interests. It’s always good to find that spark.      Absolutely. I think it’s important to keep learning and adapting, even in retirement. There's always something new to discover.      I agree. It’s interesting how our paths have crossed here, talking about something we both know a bit about. It’s a nice break from the working party, don’t you think?

Dad, I can't believe we're still stuck on this motorway. Have we gone past the last service station?      Nope, we’re still heading east. I think the next one is at junction 12. You know how these routes are—always longer than expected.      I know, I know. I’ve been counting the exits. If we don’t get off soon, we’ll miss the turn to Cornwall.      I heard you're thinking about studying philosophy next year. You know, I used to love that in school. I remember our teacher, Mr. Barnes, always said, "Philosophy isn’t just about asking questions—it's about how you answer them."      Yeah, I guess. I’m still trying to figure out if I want to do it at university. I mean, I love thinking about big ideas, but I’m also worried about the cost.      You don’t have to decide now. I’d say take your time. My degree was in English, and I still use it every day. You’ll find your path.      Thanks, Dad. I just wish I had a little more confidence. I’m so scared of failing.      Hey, don’t worry. You’ve got this. And besides, you’ve always been a quick thinker. You’ll do great.      I guess. But also, I’m trying to learn more about the language. I’m fascinated by etymology and how words evolve. Like, do you know where the word  quinoa  comes from?      I think it’s from the Quechua language. It’s a seed from the Andes, right? I remember reading that it’s a superfood, but I’ve never tried it.      Yeah, it's supposed to be healthy. I’ve seen it at the farmer’s market. I tried some once, and it was kind of weird, but I like that it’s sustainable.      Sounds like a good choice. I also love going to the farmer’s market. You can find some amazing stuff there. Speaking of markets, I remember a bike race I once saw at one in Bolton. It was wild.      You’re telling me. I saw a video online about pigs in a farmer’s market—like, they had pigs for sale? It was so weird.      Oh, I’ve seen that too. Some people get squeamish about it. I mean, I’m not a fan of organ donations, but I think it’s important to be informed.

So, what are we even having for dinner? I just pulled out a tin of beans and a tin of baked beans. I’m not sure I can cook something that involves more than a microwave.      You’re not supposed to be cooking, you’re supposed to be eating. I brought the bread, and I know Dave’s got the tomatoes. We just need to throw everything in a pan and call it a meal.      Oh, don’t forget the salad. I brought that. Although, I’m not sure how you can call it a salad if you’ve only got lettuce and cucumber. What’s the point?      My point is, I’ve already made the left-over roast beef last week, and I’m not making another one. I’ve got enough of that. Plus, I’m not a chef, I’m a conference co-ordinator.      Oh, the  confident  one. You always say that, but you’ve got more food knowledge than me. I mean, I can tell a good steak when I see one, but I’ve still got no idea how to cook it.      Well, I used to cook. Back when I had a job. I used to make these really good Sunday roasts. My mum used to say I was like a chef. If I weren’t retired, I’d be running a restaurant.      You’d have to work for it, then. I’m still waiting to see a proper roast in this house. I mean, I had one in Doncaster last year, and it was  amazing . My auntie used to cook it every Sunday.      That’s because she was a proper cook. I mean, we had to go all the way to Doncaster just to eat something decent. I can barely make a proper omelette without burning it.      I know what you mean. We used to have proper meals in our house. Even if it was just a roast and some chips, it was better than the stuff you get in a takeaway.      I think we’re missing out on something. Maybe if we all pitched in a bit, we could do something decent. I’ve got the oven, I can do the cooking, and you two could handle the clean-up.      Sounds like a plan. But only if you promise not to burn the beans this time.      Oh, I’ll do my best. I may not cook, but I can at least peel the potatoes.

So, I heard you're teaching English as a Foreign Language. That’s pretty cool. What’s it like working with students from different countries?      It’s actually really rewarding. I teach a mix of international students and locals who are looking to improve their skills. The best part is getting to learn about different cultures through their perspectives. It’s like a constant exchange of ideas.      That sounds great. I always thought teaching was more about just standing in front of a class. But I guess it’s more interactive than that, right?      Definitely. I spend a lot of time giving feedback, helping them with pronunciation, and even practicing conversations. It’s not just about grammar—it’s about communication. I mean, I’ve even had to learn a bit of Spanish and French to help my students better.      That’s impressive. I’m actually thinking about going back to school for a degree. I’ve been working as a bartender for a few years now, but I feel like I’m not using the skills I learned in uni. What did you study?      I did a postgraduate in Applied Linguistics. It was quite a focus on language acquisition and teaching methodologies. It helped me understand how people learn languages differently, which is super useful now.      That’s awesome. I’m considering something similar, maybe in education or something related. But I don’t know if I have the time. I’m already working 50 hours a week.      I get that. It’s tough balancing work and studies. But if you’re passionate about it, it’s worth it. I actually started my postgrad part-time while working, and it worked out.      That’s good to know. I’m just worried about the financial aspect. My parents aren’t too supportive of me going back to school. They think I should just stick with what I’m doing now.      I understand. It’s always a risk, but sometimes you have to take it. Plus, if you’re doing something you love, it’s not just about the money. It’s about personal growth.      True. I guess I need to talk to them more. Maybe I can show them some of the courses I’ve been looking into. It’s about time I stop settling for just a job and start thinking about something that really excites me.      That sounds like a good move.

Alright, lads, we're running late for break time. I was just making coffee when I heard the clock strike. I’m telling you, it’s not like we’ve got the time to dawdle anymore.      I know, I know. But it’s not like we’re in a rush to get anywhere. Not with the weather like this. I’ve been trying to get the plants watered, but they’re so fussy.      Yes, but it’s not just the plants. I’ve been thinking about the donation box we were talking about earlier. I’ve got a few ideas. Maybe we could put up some banners around the community center? Something about helping those in need, you know?      Banners, eh? I’ve seen them around the place. But I think we need to make sure it’s not just for show. I mean, we’ve got to mean it. You know, like a real cause.      That’s the spirit, old chap. I’ve been thinking about the Gambia, too. You remember that trip we planned? It was going to be so good. I even started saving up, but then life got in the way.      It was a shame about the Munchausen Syndrome comment, though. That was a bit of a somersault. I mean, it’s a real condition, and we don’t want to trivialize it. But someone said it in passing, and it took a while to sort out.      I don’t mind a bit of banter, but when it comes to serious topics, we need to be careful. Especially with people who’ve had such rough times.      Exactly. We’ve all been there, you know. I’ve had a few run-ins with the system, and I know how it feels to be overlooked. That’s why I think the donation box is a good idea. It’s about giving back, no matter how small.      Speaking of giving back, I was also thinking about the bell ringing. It’s been a long time since we did it together. I believe the community center is still in the process of organizing a session. I’ll reach out and see if we can get it going again.      That’d be splendid. I’ve always loved the sound of bells. It’s like a reminder that there’s still some good in the world.      And don’t forget the driving. I’ve been thinking about getting my license back.

So, I just got this new mobile app that’s supposed to help you find the best food spots in town. It’s called  TasteGuide . It’s actually pretty cool—like, it recommends places based on your preferences and even shows reviews from people in your area. I’ve already used it twice this week and found two really good places to eat.      Oh, really? That sounds amazing. I’ve been thinking about trying out more places around here, but I haven’t found a good app that actually works. I mean, I’ve tried a few, but they always seem to give me the same generic recommendations. Maybe I should try  TasteGuide ?      Yeah, I use one of those too, but I’m not sure how accurate it is. I think I tried  EatOut  once and it suggested a place that was basically a hole in the wall. I ended up going somewhere else because it was too crowded. Maybe  TasteGuide  is better.      Wait, I’ve heard of that one. I think it’s actually one of the most popular ones in the city. I might have to download it. But do you think it’s worth the subscription fee? I’m not sure if I want to pay for it just for one or two recommendations.      Hmm, I think the free version is okay, but the paid version unlocks more features like personalized recommendations and even delivery tracking. I don’t mind paying a little for convenience, especially since I’m always on the go.      I can see that. I mean, I’m not a huge fan of being crowded, but I do like to try new things. Speaking of which, I’m thinking about trying out a scary movie this weekend. I’ve been meaning to watch  Hereditary  again. It’s so intense, but it’s also really good.      Oh, I saw that one. I actually watched it last week, and it was absolutely terrifying. I couldn’t sleep for days. I even had to switch off the lights and make sure my door was locked.      Wow, I’m not sure I’m ready for that. I mean, I like a good horror movie, but I think I’d go for something a little less intense. Maybe  The Conjuring ? I remember that was really good too.      Yeah,  The Conjuring  is a classic. I’ve watched it a few times, and it never gets old.

Well, I've been meaning to talk to you about that old car of yours, Dave. You know, the one you've had since the seventies. It's not going to last much longer, is it?      Oh, come on, Tom, it’s been a good old dog. I've had more trouble with the bloody neighbors than the car! But I tell you what, I’ve been thinking about getting a new one. The old thing’s started making that grinding noise when I turn the steering wheel. It’s not safe, and I don’t fancy getting stuck on the A1 again.      You know, I heard about that noise, too. I think it's the front suspension. You should get it checked out before it’s too late. I know a guy who fixes cars in the village. He’s been recommending me for years. Maybe you could take it to him?      That’s a good idea, Liza. But I’ve been trying to get my hands on some spare cash. I’ve got this bit of savings, but I’m not sure if it’s enough. I’ve got to be careful with it. You know how it is, with the state of the economy and everything.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve got the same problem. I’ve been trying to get a bit of work here and there, but nothing comes up. I’m not one of those young lads who can just jump on a lorry and drive around. I’ve got to be careful with my health, too. I’ve had a few aches and pains over the years.      That’s true, and I understand. I’ve been childminding for years, and even then, it wasn’t easy. But I think you both should consider using the bus more. The new route goes all the way to Norwich. It’s not as slow as it used to be, and it’s more reliable. You can get a pass for the whole month, and it’s cheaper than waiting for a car to break down.      I know, Liza. I keep telling myself that I should start using the bus more, but I get this urge to drive. I mean, I’ve been driving all my life, and it’s a habit. But I suppose I should be more practical. You know, the other day I was trying to get home from the village, and the traffic was a nightmare.

So, I've been thinking about moving house again. I mean, it's not like I have anywhere to go, but it's starting to feel like I'm stuck in a loop. I saw this little cottage near the coast, only an hour from here. It's got a garden and a view. I just don’t know if I can afford it, though.      You know, I’ve been thinking about that too. I was just looking at some properties online. It's surprising how many places are still available. You could go for something smaller, even if it’s not a dream home. Just something that feels like a fresh start.      Honestly, I can relate. I’ve been thinking about changing my situation. I left the oil industry last year, and now I’m just sitting around waiting for something to happen. I mean, I used to be a technical expert, but now I feel like I’m just a ghost. Maybe I should start looking for something different.      I know what you mean. I spent decades in the classroom, and now I’m just… I don’t know. I feel like I’ve lost my purpose. I tell myself I’ll find something, but I don’t know where to start.      Maybe it’s time to take a step back. I’ve been thinking about traveling more. I mean, I did that for a while after college, and it really opened my eyes. Maybe you two could take a trip together. It would be a way to break the monotony.      That’s a good idea. I’ve been wanting to see some places in the UK, but I just haven’t had the time or money. I remember the last time I traveled, it was just a weekend trip to the countryside. I got to see the countryside, the air was so clean, and I felt like I could breathe again.      Yeah, I remember that. I used to take my students on field trips, and I always felt that connection with the land. It’s funny how something so simple can make you feel alive again.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? You don’t need a lot of money to travel. You just need to plan a little and be open to new experiences. I think it’s important to remind ourselves that life isn’t just about where we are, but what we do with it.

Mummy, do you know what happened to my bike? I was so worried it was gone for good!      I know, sweetheart. I found it this morning, tucked neatly under the porch. It looked like someone had gone to a lot of trouble to hide it, but I’m glad it’s safe.      Oh, thank goodness! I was so upset. I had to borrow my friend Lily’s bike for a week. But you know what? Her dad said he’s going to get a new one soon.      That’s good. But I think you should be more careful about where you leave your bike, especially after dark. I heard on the news that there’s been a rise in bike thefts around Hastings.      Yeah, I guess. But I didn’t think anyone would go for a bike in the daytime. I mean, it was just on the street outside my school.      It can happen anywhere, even in daylight. I remember when I was your age, I once left my bike in a parking lot and it was gone by the time I got back from the shops. It was a real shock.      Did you ever find it?      No, not that one. But I got a new one, and I made sure to lock it properly. You know, with a proper U-lock and a chain.      I’ll do that. I’ve been meaning to get a better lock. I’m even thinking about getting a smart bike lock that can be tracked on my phone.      Oh, that sounds smart! Maybe you could even use social media to post about it. I know you’ve been really into that lately.      Yeah, I tried posting about my missing bike on Instagram. A few people commented and offered help. One even mentioned they saw someone suspicious near the school.      That’s amazing. You’re getting so good at using social media. I remember when I was your age, I couldn’t even open a Facebook account without asking your dad.      You were so strict about that! But I guess it’s good that I’m learning how to use it properly.      Exactly. And remember, even if you can’t find your bike, there’s always a way to get a new one. Just like I did.      I know. I’m just glad it’s back. I can’t wait to ride it again.      Me too.

So, I've just finished making the lasagna, and I think it's going to be awesome. I got the fresh pasta from the local market, and the meat sauce was something I made from scratch. It’s been ages since we had a proper meal like this at the cottage.      That sounds delicious, Sarah. I was just thinking about the train trip we had last week. I remember that one time when the train got stuck in a tunnel for over an hour, and we had to wait with a bunch of people in the dark. It was a bit eerie, but we made the best of it.      Oh, that sounds like one of those stories we can add to the family legend. I remember my Uncle Dave telling me about a time when he was on the train and the conductor lost his ticket. The whole carriage had to get off and walk to the next station. It was a nightmare, but he said it was like a comedy in real life.      Ah, the train stories always bring the memories. I still remember the time I was on the way to visit my cousin in Cardiff, and the train broke down in the countryside. We ended up getting picked up by a farmer and driven for miles. It was a little chaotic, but it turned out to be one of the best travel experiences I’ve had.      I don’t know about you all, but I’d rather be stuck on a train than dealing with the supermarkets. Last week, I tried to buy some cheese, and the line was so long, I ended up losing my patience and just bought a bag of chips instead. I feel like I’m becoming a bit of a food conspiracy theorist.      I can relate to that. I think it’s all about the stress of daily life. But I’m trying to be more mindful. I’ve started cooking more for the family, and it’s actually making me feel more connected. Plus, I think it’s a great way to unwind after a long week.      That’s such a good point. Cooking together can be a great bonding activity. I think we should organize a weekly dinner night. Maybe even set a theme each week. Like Italian one night, Mexican another. It could be fun and help us all learn new things.

So, I've been thinking about our last game of Catan. You were so competitive, just like you always are. I swear, you’re like a professional player in your own right.      Oh, come on, I was just trying to win. You know how I get during games. It’s like my inner competitiveness comes out. But honestly, I think you’re not giving yourself enough credit. You’re actually pretty good at strategy.      Thanks, but I think you’re just saying that because you don’t want to admit I’ve been getting better. I mean, I’ve been studying the rules and everything. I even read the strategy guide you left on the shelf.      Oh, I left it there? I thought I had taken it back to my flat. Hmm, maybe I should have kept it with me. Anyway, you’re better than you give yourself credit for. I mean, you’ve been getting better at planning your settlements and trading resources.      I know, I know. It’s just that I still feel like I need to prove myself. I mean, we both know you’ve been playing board games for years. You’ve got this whole library of strategy guides and game theory books.      Yeah, but I think you’re catching up fast. I mean, you’ve got this natural way of thinking ahead. Maybe it’s because you’re a lecturer? I mean, you’re always analyzing situations and thinking critically.      That’s one way to put it. Although, I think it’s more about how I’ve been spending my free time. I’ve been watching a lot of documentary series about game design and the psychology of play. It’s fascinating.      That’s cool. I’ve been thinking about getting into game design myself. Maybe I should try my hand at creating something. I mean, I know a lot about the mechanics, but I’ve never actually designed a full game.      That sounds like a great idea. I mean, we could even collaborate. You could take care of the mechanics and strategy, and I could handle the storytelling and aesthetics.      I like the sound of that. I think it could be a fun project. And who knows, maybe we could even test it out with our friends. Although, I might have to start by getting some proper materials.      Yeah, that’s a good start. It’s funny how we talk about games and culture all the time, and now it’s becoming something more.

So, I just got an email from the council about the bins. They said we need to switch to the new green bins for recycling. I was like,  what?  I thought we’d been doing this for ages. Do we even know what the rules are now?      Yeah, I remember when they first introduced the bins, and it was all so confusing. I think they made a big mess of it. At first, we were putting everything in the wrong bin, and then it got so complicated. I ended up just throwing everything into the black bin. It was the easiest way.      Oh, I still can’t get my head around it. I mean, I have a bit of a green thumb, but even I get confused. It’s like they want to make recycling harder, not easier. I’ve been trying to find a clear guide, but everything’s just a jumble of terms— kerbside, re-cycling, waste-stream…  It’s like they’re speaking a different language.      Exactly! I was thinking about moving house, you know? I’ve been looking at some properties in the area. It’s not the easiest time to move, especially with the bins and all. I mean, if I have to sort through all that at the new place, I might as well just throw it all in the black bin. I’m not sure I want to deal with that again.      I can imagine. I was just telling Sarah the other day about the time I accidentally put a pizza box in the green bin. I got a letter saying I was in breach of the recycling regulations. Can you believe it? I had to call the council about it. They finally sent someone to check the bins, and it turned out I’d just made a mistake. Still, that was a bit of a hassle.      Oh, I’ve heard that story. It’s like they’re trying to make sure everyone is  just  right. But honestly, I think there’s a way to make it more accessible. We need to have clearer signs and maybe even some sort of community guide. I’m a bit of a crafts person, so I could even make a poster or something for the neighbors.      That’s a great idea! Maybe we could start a little neighborhood initiative. It would be good to have a group of people who can help each other out.

Okay, so we’re supposed to go via the A12? I thought it would be quicker to take the A10, but I guess this is the recommended route.      I know what you mean. I used to take the A10 every time, but the traffic got so bad that I started taking the A12. It’s a bit longer, but less stressful. Plus, I got used to the longer routes.      Yeah, and when you're in London, the traffic is like a constant battle. I remember my first time driving through the city, I thought I was going to end up in a complete gridlock.      Oh, I remember that too. It’s like the city has a mind of its own. I was driving with my cousin once, and we got stuck in a queue for over an hour. The traffic light was just sitting there, and we had to wait for it to turn green.      That sounds like a nightmare. I mean, we’re not even in the city anymore. We’re in East London, but I can already feel it.      Speaking of the city, I was thinking about France again today. You know, the trip we were planning. I sent an email to the travel agent, and they said they have some great deals on train tickets.      That’s great! I was really looking forward to going. I think I want to bring some books with me, you know, for the train ride.      That’s a good idea. I was just thinking about the TLS. I got a new subscription last month, and it’s been fantastic. I read so much more now.      Yeah, digital vs. print is such a debate. I still prefer print, but I can see the convenience of digital. Though, I do miss the feel of a real book.      I know what you mean. I’ve tried a few e-readers, but nothing beats the smell of paper and the sound of pages turning.      I can’t wait to get to North London. I have a few errands to run, and after that, I’m going to visit my aunt. She’s been meaning to give me a present, and I think she’s finally got something ready.      That’s nice. I hope it’s something special. You always deserve a gift, especially after all the hard work you’ve been doing.      Thanks, Mum. I really appreciate it.

So, I was in the Lake District last summer, and I thought I’d try that hike up Scafell Pike. I’m like, “Okay, I can do this,” and then I’m halfway up, and I’m like, “I’m not actually doing this.”      Classic you, mate. You always think you’ve got the stamina. I’ve heard about your “Scafell Pike moment” from the whole pub.      Yeah, and when you got halfway up, you started texting your mum for help. I still remember you saying, “Mum, I’m not going to die, I just need a bit of encouragement.”      And then she sent back, “You’ll be fine, love. Just don’t forget your hat.” You were wearing one?      No, I wasn’t. I was trying to keep it light, you know. But the wind was so strong, I thought I was going to get blown off the mountain.      You were like a leaf on the wind. One second you’re standing there, and the next, you’re “flown” – no pun intended.      Yeah, yeah, don’t get all emotional. I’ve got a story too. Last summer, I went to the coast with my mates. We rented a van and tried to do a road trip.      Oh, what happened?      We got stuck in a village called Blyth. No signal, no petrol, and it was midday. We tried to call a cab, but the only person who answered was a guy who said, “I’m not letting you in.”      Sounds like a classic British small-town encounter.      I could see it. Like,  you  being the only one with a mobile phone, and the whole village looking at you like you’re the enemy.      Yeah, go on, tell us how you got out of it.      Well, I had to improvise. I said, “Mate, I’m not trying to be rude, but I really need a ride.” And he said, “You’re not from around here, are you?”      I’m guessing he didn’t let you in.      No, he said, “I’ll give you a lift if you buy me a pint.” And I thought, “Yeah, right, I’ll buy you a pint, and then I’ll get to the next town.”      That’s the kind of courage that gets you through life.      To the road trip tales and the villagers who test your spirit.      To the mountains that test your limits and the pubs that save you.

So, I've been thinking about taking up wild winter camping. I know it's a bit of a niche hobby, but I've been reading up on it and I'm really intrigued.      Oh, wild winter camping? I've heard of it, but I haven't really considered it myself. I mean, I do love the outdoors, but the idea of sleeping in the cold? I'm not sure I'd have the grit for it.      You'd be surprised. It’s not just about the cold—it's about being in tune with nature, being self-sufficient, and pushing your limits. I've done a few trips in the Scottish Highlands, and it's an amazing experience.      That sounds incredible. I grew up in London, so I’ve never really had the chance to get out into the wild much. But I’ve always been curious. I mean, I’ve spent years in research, and I’ve read a lot about the science of nature and how it affects the mind. It makes sense why people would want to disconnect from the city and immerse themselves in something raw like that.      That's interesting. I'm a nurse, so I deal with people's mental health quite a bit. I've seen how nature can really help with stress and anxiety, and I think wild camping could be a powerful tool for some. But I wonder if it's for everyone. I mean, you need to be physically prepared, and mentally too.      Absolutely. It's not for the faint-hearted. But if you're up for it, the rewards are huge. I remember one time I was in the Cairngorms, and the silence was so profound. No phones, no distractions, just the wind and the stars. It's like you’re reminded of how small you are, and how connected you are to something bigger.      That must be a humbling experience. I can see how it could be therapeutic. I've been thinking about trying it myself, but I'm a bit nervous about the logistics. How do you even start?      You start small. Maybe a weekend trip, just a couple of nights. You don't have to go into the wilderness entirely. Even a weekend in the countryside can be a step in the right direction. It builds your confidence.      Exactly. And you don't have to go it alone.

So, I just watched this film called  The Last Tree —you know, the one with that British actor from  Peaky Blinders ? It was pretty intense, actually. I didn’t expect it to be so… heavy.      Yeah, I saw that too. I mean, it’s got that sort of gritty, realistic vibe that always gets me thinking about environmental issues. But I didn’t think it’d hit me so hard. I mean, I’m a consultant engineer, so I see a lot of infrastructure projects, but this made me question how much we’re really doing to preserve what’s left.      I know, right? It’s like, you think you’re contributing to the future, but then you see something like that and it makes you realize how much we’re losing. It reminded me of that book I read last year— The Overstory  by Richard Powers. You ever read that? It’s about trees, but it’s also about human relationships with nature.      I have! I read it over the summer. I was really into it, but I found it a bit slow at first. But once it got going, it was impossible to put down. I even got a bit emotional during the ending.      Oh, I know. I cried. I mean, I’m not one to burst into tears over books, but that part where the tree is still standing after all those years—it just felt like a symbol of hope.      Exactly. That’s what I love about literature. It can make you feel something deeply, even if it’s not the most straightforward story. I mean, I’ve been working on a few projects lately that involve sustainable development, so it’s good to have that perspective.      That’s cool. I know you’re always up for a challenge. I mean, your job’s got to be interesting. Do you get to travel a lot?      Not too much, but I do get to meet some really cool people. I was in Manchester last week for a conference. The food there is amazing—especially the fish and chips. You ever been?      Yeah, I’ve had it in Sunderland. That’s where I’m from. It’s not the same as Manchester, though. I mean, it’s got that real, gritty charm, you know?      I can imagine. I’ve been to a few places in the North, and I’ve always liked the food there.

So, I was telling the kids about that time I tried to write a story on a typewriter. I had no idea how it worked. I thought it was like a keyboard, but it just made all sorts of noise and the letters didn’t even come out right.      Did you use one of those old things with the paper roll? Like the ones you see in old movies?      Exactly! And I used Excel to track my progress. I thought it would help me stay organized. But honestly, it was a complete mess. I had the story in one cell, and I kept changing it, and the spreadsheet kept getting all confused.      I remember you telling us about that! You said you accidentally wrote the story in the wrong language.      Oh, that’s right! I had a British accent in one paragraph and a French accent in the next. It was like the characters were arguing with each other.      You were trying to write a story about a group of kids who went on a treasure hunt, weren’t you?      Yes! It was supposed to be a fantasy story, with a map and a secret cave. But I got so distracted trying to figure out the typewriter and Excel that the plot just… faded away.      You should’ve made it a Lego story instead. You could’ve built the cave with blocks.      Yeah, and you could’ve used the PlayStation to play through the story like a game. I’ve seen those interactive adventure games.      That’s true. I remember when I first played a game where you had to solve puzzles to move forward. It felt like a real adventure. I wish I could’ve tried that with the kids.      You know, I was thinking about the Brownie Promise evening we had last week. I told the story about the brave girl who saved the village.      Oh, that was good. I remember the kids were so into it. They even wanted to know if the girl had a go-kart or something.      I think they wanted to be the hero, not the girl.      Maybe they’re just waiting for the right story. I think I’ll start writing one with them. Maybe about a potion that turns Legos into real things.      That sounds like a perfect bedtime story.      Right. And we’ll make sure to keep the Excel sheet updated.

You know, I’ve been meaning to ask—what’s with all the scruffy clothes lately? You look like you’ve been living in a box for the last week.      Oh, it’s just the weather, mate. It’s been so damp out there, I’ve been wearing my old jumpers and trousers just to keep warm. Plus, I’ve been getting up late, so I just throw on whatever’s easiest. It’s not like I’m going anywhere fancy.      I can see that. Though I still can’t get over how you managed to keep your hair so clean despite all that. You must have a secret.      Yeah, I tried growing herbs in the back garden. Dill, parsley, even some thyme. But then the roadworks started, and the noise drove me mad. I gave up after a week. Still, it’s a bit of a hobby, you know.      I’ve been thinking about growing some herbs myself, maybe even some fruit. My cousin in Devon has a small fruit farm, and she’s got the most beautiful apples. She says they’re perfect for making jam.      Jam? You’re not seriously thinking of making your own, are you? I’ve seen the state of your kitchen. It’s like a war zone.      Well, it’s either that or buying jam from the supermarket, which I can’t stand. I mean, who wants factory-made jam? It’s got no soul.      I know what you mean. My mum always made her own jam, and it was the best. She even had this old recipe that used to take days to prepare. Though I can’t do that now. I’ve got a job that keeps me busy.      Speaking of busy, I heard there’s a lot of junk mail going around. We get it all the time. Some of it’s even from people we’ve never met.      Oh, don’t even start. I’ve got a box full of it. I think the postman’s trying to get me to sell my house. I’ve got that old property in the countryside, you know.      I heard about that. You’re going to sell it, aren’t you?      Maybe. I’ve been thinking about it. I’m not really staying there anymore. It’s too much work, and I’m just not the same person I used to be.      I get that.

So, I was just telling my sister about the time I tried to cook a Christmas dinner without any help. I ended up burning the turkey and over-seasoning the gravy. It was a disaster, but I think the kids thought it was a joke.      That sounds like something I’d do. I once tried to make a roast chicken for my wife’s birthday and forgot to preheat the oven. The chicken was raw inside and burnt on the outside. She still laughs about it.      Honestly, I’d rather just order takeaway. I’ve tried cooking more than once and always end up with something that tastes like a mystery. But I do love trying new recipes when I’m in the mood. It’s just that I’m not the best at following instructions.      I get that. I’m better at breakfasts—like eggs and toast. But when it comes to main meals, I’m not so confident. Speaking of food, have you ever tried the local Christmas market in Ashford? I heard it’s amazing.      Yes! I went last year and got some really good mulled wine. The food was great, and it was such a nice way to spend the holidays. I even got a gift for my mum there. It’s a great place to find unique Christmas presents.      That’s a good idea. I’ve never been to one, but I should check them out. I was thinking about buying my daughter a new phone for Christmas. Do you think I should get her the latest model or stick with something more practical?      That depends on what she needs. If she’s always using her phone for work, maybe the latest is better. But if she’s more into social media, something with a better camera might be useful. I’d say go for the latest model. She’ll appreciate the extra features.      Yeah, I think the latest is a safe choice. I got my phone last year, and it’s been great. I use it for work and staying in touch with friends. Oh, and I’ve been trying to learn how to use the new features on my camera app. It’s pretty cool.      You’re always learning something new. I’ve been trying to figure out how to use the voice assistant on my phone. I keep accidentally telling it to play music instead of setting reminders.

So, how's life treating you these days? I feel like ages since we last caught up. You know, since the last time we were in that tiny café in Wimbledon.      Oh, you remember that! It was like a war zone in there. But hey, it’s been a while. Work’s been keeping me on my toes. I’ve been doing some part-time programming for a survey company, just to keep the cash flowing while I finish my postgrad. It’s not easy, but it’s manageable.      I can only imagine. You’re in a higher professional bracket, so I guess you’ve got a bit more stability than I do. I’m still bouncing around the copywriting scene, trying to land that big agency gig. It’s all very glamorous on the surface, but the hours are brutal.      Yeah, I hear you. I envy you for the creative side, but honestly, I’d kill for a bit more structure. I mean, you know how it is—feeling like you’re always chasing the next project.      Totally. I’m also trying to figure out my future plans. I’ve been thinking about moving back to Kent, near my family. I miss the countryside, you know? Even though it’s got a bit of a ‘nothing much happens’ vibe.      That sounds nice. You know, I’ve been thinking about that too. There’s something about being close to family that makes you feel grounded. Though, honestly, I can’t wait to get out of this flat. It’s like a prison with a view.      That’s a good point. I’ve been trying to save up for a deposit, but with the cost of living where it is, it’s not easy. I mean, it’s not like I’m not trying, but it feels like every time I save a bit, it disappears somewhere.      I know the feeling. I’ve tried cutting back on things, but honestly, the bills just keep coming. Though, I did manage to get a side hustle with the survey work—some of the people pay really well for their opinions.      That’s clever. I need to figure out something like that. Maybe I can find a niche in the copywriting world. I’ve been thinking about writing for local businesses, you know? It’s not as glamorous, but it’s more stable.      That’s a solid plan.

So, I've been thinking about getting back into exercise. I've been feeling a bit sluggish lately. I used to go to the gym every now and then, but it's been a while. Maybe I should try something different, like yoga or swimming?      That sounds like a good idea. I’ve been trying to be more active too. I’ve started going for walks with my dog every morning. It’s actually quite refreshing. I’ve even taken up some light jogging on weekends.      Oh, I love that! I’ve been doing yoga almost every evening. It’s not just about the physical exercise—it’s also a great way to unwind and clear my mind. I’ve been working on a new project, and it’s been so stressful. Yoga helps me stay grounded.      That’s really smart. I’ve heard a lot about the mental benefits of yoga, but I’ve never tried it. Maybe I should give it a shot. I’ve also been thinking about starting to cook more at home. I’ve been relying too much on takeaway and convenience meals, and I feel like it’s affecting my health.      I completely agree. Cooking at home is such a good habit. I’ve been experimenting with healthy recipes lately. I’ve even started growing some herbs in my kitchen. It’s fun and adds a nice touch to meals. What kind of cooking are you interested in?      I’m into all kinds of cooking, but I’ve been focusing more on simple, wholesome meals lately. I’ve been making a lot of soups and stews, and I’ve started using more vegetables. I’ve been reading a few cookbooks about plant-based diets. It’s been quite the learning curve, but I’m really enjoying it.      That sounds amazing. I’ve always wanted to cook more, but I’ve never really had the time or confidence. Maybe I should start with something simple, like a one-pot meal or a pasta dish. I’ve been meaning to try making my own pasta.      That’s a great start. I think a little bit of experimentation is key. I’ve been making homemade pasta too—though I’m still not the best at it. It’s a bit of a process, but it’s worth it when you get it right.      Exactly! And the more you cook, the better you get.

So, I've been meaning to ask you, how's everything going with your new project? I heard you got promoted to lead the bridge design on that new residential complex in Milton Keynes.      Thanks, it's pretty exciting, honestly. The team's great, and I get to work with some really talented people. But let me ask you—how's the budget stuff going over at the university? I know you've been working on that grant application for the new research center.      Oh, it's a bit of a rollercoaster. We've had some pushback from the funding body about the scope, but I think we’re on the right track. Honestly, it’s been one of the most challenging but rewarding projects I’ve worked on.      That sounds intense. I’ve been trying to keep up with the budget changes myself. It’s a bit of a nightmare trying to track where every penny goes. Speaking of which, have you heard anything about the recent budget announcements?      Yeah, I did. They’re cutting a lot of funding for arts and humanities, which is a shame. Especially with the upcoming musicals season at the Cambridge Festival. I was really looking forward to that.      That’s a bummer. I heard they’re pushing for more STEM-focused events now. But I still think musicals are important. You know, they're not just entertainment—they bring people together, and they’re a big part of our culture.      Absolutely. I mean, think about the talent that goes into a musical—actors, directors, set designers, all working together. It’s like a collaborative art form. I’ve been trying to get the university to sponsor a few student productions.      That sounds like a great idea. You should definitely push for it. I’ll even help you draft a proposal if you want. I’ve got some experience with grant writing from my engineering projects.      Really? That would be amazing. We could really use someone with your background. Also, have you been to any good musicals lately? I’ve been thinking about going to  West Side Story  at the theatre in the city.      I haven’t seen one in a while, but I’m actually going to see  Les Misérables  this weekend. I think it’s playing at the Cambridge Arts Theatre. Want to come?      That sounds like a plan. I’ll talk to the team and let them know I’ll be unavailable for a few hours.

Alright, I've got the brushes and the paint, but I still can’t get the colour right. It’s supposed to be a nice moss green for the fence, but it looks like a swamp.      You know, I used to paint the cabs when I was younger. I reckon the key is to mix it with some white. Otherwise, it just looks too dark and gloomy.      Huh, I never thought about that. I was just pulling straight from the can. Maybe I should check the instructions again.      That’s the problem with second-hand stuff. You never know what you’re getting. I bought a few bits and bobs from a market last week, and half of it was useless.      Exactly. But some of the stuff is good. Like that old ladder I got from a friend. It’s still strong and doesn’t wobble.      Speaks volumes for the person who gave it to you. I got a broken ladder once, and I had to borrow one from a neighbour. He said it was fine, but it ended up bending in the middle.      I remember watching a film about a guy who was a humble mechanic. He used to fix everything, from cars to furniture. He had this way of looking at problems that made everything seem solvable.      That’s the spirit. I’ve always believed in fixing things instead of throwing them away. My dad taught me that. He used to say, “If it’s broken, it’s just waiting to be fixed.”      That’s a great philosophy. It’s about responsibility, too. I mean, the gutters are leaking again. I’ve been meaning to fix them, but I’m not sure if it’s worth the time.      I’d say it’s worth it. A few hours of work and you’ve got a roof over your head. Plus, it’s better than waiting for the rain to damage the walls.      You’re right. I should get to it before the next storm. Speaking of storms, do you think the council will approve the new development nearby?      No way. They’re building a shopping centre just south of the town. It’s going to change the whole area. Some people are excited, others are worried about the effect on the local businesses.      Yeah, I’ve heard the same. It’s a bit of a dilemma. On one hand, it’s good for the economy, but on the other, it might push out the old shops.      Exactly.

So, I just saw this really weird sign off the highway. It said “Restroom and Biergarten” in big, blocky letters. I almost pulled over just to see what a  biergarten  is. You know, like a beer garden? But it was in the middle of nowhere.      Oh, you’re not the only one. I’ve seen that sign a few times on the way. I think it’s just a place where they serve beer and have some sort of bar. Maybe it’s not even open? Or maybe it’s just a prank.      I guess. But honestly, I’m just hoping we’ll find a proper café before we hit Tarnow. I’ve been living off cereal and left-over sandwiches for the last two days. I’m starting to feel like a sad, single dad who’s lost his job and his will to live.      Ha! Don’t say that. You’re not a single dad. You’re just a qualified teacher who’s taking a sabbatical. Or at least pretending to be. Come on, we’ve got a place booked in Tarnow. You’ll have a proper meal.      Yeah, but I still feel like I’m paying too much for this trip. My last job was at a language school in Cambridge, and I was getting paid more than this. It’s not fair. I mean, I’m not even sure what I’m doing here. I just wanted to travel, and now I’m sitting in a campervan with a friend who’s got a steady job and is going to a conference in Poland.      Look, I know you’re feeling about this. But you’re not unemployed. You’re just... waiting. And I think this trip is helping. You know, clearing the clutter. I’ve been doing that too. I used to work in a school, but I got promoted to a managerial role. It wasn’t me. I felt like I was just checking boxes.      You’re right. I think I need to figure out what I want to do with my life again. I’ve been thinking about teaching again, but I don’t know where. Maybe I should travel more and see what I can find.      That’s a good idea. You’re not the only one who’s been feeling the need to clear the clutter. I think we’re both at that point in life where we need to take a step back and figure out what we truly want.

So, are we really going all the way to Preston just for some groceries? I mean, the supermarket in St Anne’s is like, 20 minutes away.      I know, I know—  but   we’re getting a bit of a detour to pick up some things for the Hay Festival. You know, the books, the author meet-and-greets, the whole vibe.      Yeah, and it’s not just about the books. You know how much the kids get excited about it. It’s like, every year it’s  this  week, and we’ve got to make sure we’re in town early.      Oh, come on, the Hay Festival is  yearly  and I think it’s in Wales. So why are we going all the way to Preston, which is in England?      Oh, you’re not thinking clearly. The Hay Festival isn’t in Wales, it’s in  Powys . But we’re going to Preston because the last time we did the festival, we had to move the car twice because of the train strikes and the roads were  packed .      And then we had to wait in line for three hours to get into the cheapest ticket. It was madness.      I’d rather wait in line for a book at the library. Honestly, I don’t know why we bother. I mean, the only reason I’d ever go is if someone was giving a talk on  Harry Potter  or something.      Don’t say that! You’re missing out. You know what you’re missing? The chance to meet actual authors and have real conversations about books.      And if you’re not careful, you might even end up meeting someone you used to know from school. I tried to find my old English teacher last year. She had a  blog  now.      Oh, come on, you’re not telling me you still talk to her?      Don’t be silly. She’s still got that air of superiority. I’m still figuring out how to talk to her without getting annoyed.      Oh, I think I know what you mean. I’m still trying to win her back. She said something about my PhD last year and it was  so  rude.      Right, so, to recap: we’re going to Preston for the Hay Festival, we’re going to do some shopping, and we might run into my English teacher.      Sounds like a plan. Just don’t forget to bring your book list.

Well, I've just got back from the shops, and I was trying to buy some cleaning products. I got to the end of the aisle, and there was a sign saying, “Clearance: All items 50% off.” I thought, “Oh, brilliant, I can get a bargain!” I grabbed the first thing I saw—a bottle of bleach. I paid, and then I thought, “Wait a minute, I’m not even sure if this is the right one.” But I thought, “What’s the point of being a retired teacher if you can’t chase a bit of a bargain?”      Ha! I remember when I was teaching, I used to joke that we were all like that—trying to get the best deal on everything. I even tried to negotiate with the shopkeeper once, and he looked at me like I was from another planet.      Yeah, but Grandpa, you’re the one who bought the last bottle of hairspray from the bin. You told me it was “from the era of the Queen’s reign.” I still don’t know if it works or not.      Ah, that was a  great  purchase! I washed my hair with it, and it looked like a raccoon had been in there. But I swear, it smelled like the 70s. I think I’ve got some kind of nostalgia tic now.      I don’t know, it’s kind of charming. I think nostalgia is a mental illness. You know, the kind that makes you think your childhood was better than it actually was. I’ve been reading about it—some call it “the feeling of being stuck in a time machine.”      Does that mean I have it too? I keep trying to fix my Xbox with a hairdryer. I’m convinced it’s going to work.      Oh, I know what you mean. I tried to fix my television once with a wooden spoon. I don’t know what I was thinking. My daughter laughed so hard she cried.      It’s amazing how the older you get, the more you believe in things you don’t even understand. I think it’s called “the go-with-the-flow syndrome.” You just let life happen to you, and you try not to overthink it.      But what if it’s not happening the right way? Like, what if I’m failing my exams? I’m scared I’ll have to go into the workforce or something.

So, mate, I’ve been trying to get my new laptop to work properly, and it’s like it’s got a mind of its own. I think it might be a hardware issue, but I’m not sure. You know how I’ve been gaming a bit more lately, so I thought I’d finally upgrade.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I had that same problem with my last laptop. It would randomly crash when I was working on editing videos. It was a nightmare. Did you try running any diagnostics?      You know, I’ve got a guy who fixes computers down the road—his name’s Steve. He’s got this thing where he can figure out what’s wrong with a laptop just by looking at it. Maybe you should take it to him?      I was thinking about that, actually. But I wanted to test it out with you guys first. I mean, I’ve been using it for a few days now, and it’s been mostly fine. Except when I try to open some of the old games I downloaded. They get stuck on loading screens.      You’ve got to remember, though, that some older games might not be compatible with newer hardware. I mean, I tried running a few retro games on my new setup, and they actually worked better than on my old one. But maybe you could try running them through a compatibility mode or something?      Or you could just stick with the classics. I’ve been getting into a lot of old-school stuff lately—like those original DOS games. It’s like stepping back in time. You know, I even found a few of them on YouTube with walkthroughs.      That’s a good point. I’ve been trying to get into that too. I mean, it’s funny how people still talk about those old games like they’re something special. I remember my brother used to play them all the time. He used to say they were the best.      Yeah, he’s still into that stuff. He’s even started making some of his own pixel art. It’s incredible. He’s got a YouTube channel where he posts these amazing tutorials.      I’d love to see that. I mean, I’ve been into gaming for years, but I never thought about making my own stuff. Maybe I should try it.

So, how do you like the bistro? It’s quite different from anything I’ve seen in England, isn’t it? The décor is all modern, and I can’t get over the lighting. It feels like a cross between a café and a bar.      I’ve been dying to try it out. I think it’s actually pretty good. The menu is all local Polish dishes with a few international options too. I ordered the pierogi, and it was delicious. It’s surprising how much it feels like home, even though it’s in Poland.      That’s interesting. I guess it’s because we’re both used to English-style pubs, right? But I have to say, I still miss the pubs back home. There’s something about the community feel. I used to work in one, and I think I lost touch with people because of it.      You know, I’ve been thinking about that too. I used to work in a school in Manchester, and even though I love teaching, sometimes I feel like I’m not really living my dream. I mean, I’ve always wanted to travel and teach English abroad, like you did. But then, after a few years, I felt like I was stuck in a cycle.      I get that. I was in the same boat. I used to teach part-time in Cambridge, and then I got laid off. It was a tough time. I ended up doing some private lessons here and there, but it wasn’t enough to keep me going. I think I’ve been struggling with addiction, too. It’s hard to stay motivated when you feel like you’re not in control of your life.      That’s really tough. I’ve been trying to work on my fitness and my mental health. I know it’s not easy, but I think it’s the only way I can start feeling like myself again. I’ve even been going to the gym a few times a week. It’s helping me clear my head.      That’s great. I’ve been meaning to start something like that. I’ve been stuck in this cycle of unemployment and self-doubt for too long. I think I need to find a new identity, not just as a teacher, but as someone who’s still capable of making a difference in the world.

So, I've got my ticket for the Dorset Steam Fair sorted, just in time for the weekend. It's been on my list for ages, and I finally got around to buying it. The prices are reasonable, I think.      Lucky you! I was just talking to my neighbor about that. He said they’ve been raising prices every year, so it’s not as cheap as it used to be. But I guess it’s a local event, so they can afford to charge a bit more.      You know, I’ve been wanting to go too, but I’ve been worried about the facilities for people with mobility issues. I’ve got my aunt who uses a wheelchair, and I don’t want her to feel left out.      Oh, I heard they’ve been improving the access over the years. I think they’ve added more ramps and better signage. But if you’re worried, you can always ask at the ticket office for details. They might have some specific information for people with disabilities.      That’s a good idea. I’d say it’s worth checking out. I’ve heard from some friends who’ve gone before that the fair is pretty family-friendly. They even have a pet section, I think.      Yeah, I remember seeing that on the website. They have a pet enclosure where you can walk your dog, and even feed them some treats. My cat isn’t big on people, but I guess it’s a chance to let my dog socialize.      Speaking of pets, my cat has been acting up lately. I think she’s just been feeling bored because it’s been so rainy lately. I’ve started letting her out more, but I worry about her getting too used to the outside.      She’s a clever cat, then. I had a cat once that would always sit by the window and watch the birds. She used to meow like she was trying to talk to them.      That’s adorable. I’ve got a rescue cat, and she’s pretty much the same. She’s got a bit of an attitude, but she’s a good listener.      I bet. I think it’s amazing how much cats can bond with their humans. I’ve been thinking about moving some furniture around in the flat, though. It’s been a bit cluttered, and I want to make more space for my cat to roam.

Well, I've just got a letter from the council. They say they're moving us out of this old bungalow in Kendal. It's been our home for over thirty years, and I'm not sure I can bear to leave it.      That’s tough, isn’t it? I can imagine how attached you must be to that place. But I’m sure it’s for the best. A fresh start, new surroundings. Maybe you’ll find something easier to maintain.      Yeah, but moving house is always a hassle. Especially when you’re older and not used to all this tech stuff. I mean, I barely know how to use a smartphone, let alone sort out a new address and all that paperwork!      Oh, come on, you're not that old. I think you’re just being dramatic. I’ve moved twice since I was thirty, and I still remember the first time I had to drive to a new post office. It was a nightmare, but I survived.      You say that now, but I’m not sure I’d survive this one. I’m already nervous about the school term starting and the new kid who sits next to me. I don't know if I can keep up.      You’ll be fine, love. It’s all part of growing up. I remember when I was your age and I used to worry about everything. So, I was just telling Ashaad’s mum that her daughter, Emily, has a real talent for math. Last week, she solved this complex problem in class, and the teacher was stunned. It’s funny, really. So, I've been thinking about our old flat in Ashford—it's been years since we moved out. So, I was just telling the others about that time I used to cycle around the countryside when I was a kid. I remember one long ride, like 20 miles, all the way from Almondsbury to the Cotswolds. That sounds like a good time. I remember when I was a dentist, there were all sorts of perks. It was a different world back then. I even got a few free trips to places like Prague. I still have a photo of me in the Charles Bridge, taken a few years back.      Prague, right? I thought it was a great bargain trip. We went last summer, and it was like stepping back in time. The architecture, the old buildings, everything had this charm. We even found a local theatre that was fully booked, but we managed to get in by offering the usher a bottle of wine.      That’s the way to do it. I remember a time when you could just walk into a theatre or an exhibition without a ticket. Not sure how that works anymore.      I think we’re planning a jive event at the old converted barn near the park. It’s going to be a community thing—sort of a revival of the old town spirit. We’re trying to rebrand the place, you see. It used to be a vibrant spot, but it’s been ruined by all the changes.

So, I've been thinking about expanding my tutoring business. I've had a few clients asking about preparing for online exams and using social media to find study groups. So, I was just thinking about our trip to the coast last summer. Remember how we walked along that cliff path and got soaked by that sudden shower?      Oh, how could I forget! I still have that beach towel in the airing cupboard — it’s been there since then. I swear it’s still slightly damp.      It's amazing how that one day turned into such a memorable experience. I mean, we got drenched, but we also saw this incredible view of the sea at sunset. I don’t think I’ve ever seen the sky that color before.      You’re not the only one. I told my brother about it, and he said it was like something out of a postcard. I even tried to take a photo, but the rain ruined it.      That’s the thing about the sea — it’s always changing. One moment it’s calm, the next it’s stormy. I remember our friend Ellie saying something about how the sea is like a living thing. You can’t really control it, can you?      Exactly. You know, after a long week of lectures and grading, there’s nothing like the sound of the waves to remind you that life doesn’t have to be so stressful.      Absolutely. It’s funny how something as simple as the sea can have such a profound effect on us. I sometimes wonder what it would be like to live by the coast full-time. Maybe we should plan another trip soon.

So, what do you think about that new fashion line from ASOS? I saw it on the telly earlier—so much bold colour and graphic designs. I’m thinking of getting a few pieces for my sister’s birthday. Well, if you’re going to experiment, you might as well go all out! I mean, if you’re going to get a denim jacket with patches, go for it. I just need to find a pair of jeans that actually fit.      I’ll help you with that. I’ve got a few pairs I could lend you. But honestly, it’s about having fun with fashion. We’re all just trying to find our own style, right?

So, I was just telling my mum about the photos I took at the beach last weekend. I thought I had captured the perfect shot of the sunset, but when I got home, I realized I’d accidentally taken the picture upside down!      Oh, I know exactly what you mean. I once handed over a photo to my sister thinking it was a masterpiece, only to find out I’d flipped it. I felt so silly.      Yeah, and I was so proud too. I even called it “The Golden Hour” on my Instagram. It was a disaster! But I guess it’s funny now.      You know, I used to take photos all the time when I was in college. I was in the photography club, and we’d go out every weekend. I even had an old camera that I used to take pictures of the campus.      That sounds cool! Do you still do it?      Not as much now. I’m too busy with work, but I still enjoy it when I can. I think I’m going to start a little project this summer—documenting the town as it changes.      That sounds amazing. I’d love to help!      You could, but you’d have to be more serious about it.      I’ll take that as a compliment.      Okay, but seriously, you’re a good photographer. I can tell. You just need to work on your angles and not get too excited.      I am excited! That’s what makes it fun!      Sure, sure. But maybe you should be careful with your fears too. You know, like the one you mentioned last time about public speaking.      Don’t remind me. I told you I was fine.      You were fine. We just need to stop being so hard on ourselves.      I know. It’s just… I get so nervous when I’m in front of people. Sometimes I think about the time I had to give a presentation in college and I forgot my slides.      Oh, I remember that. You stood there for five minutes, trying to remember what you were going to say.      And you all laughed at me.      Well, you were funny. We all laughed, and then you came back with a great presentation.      Yeah, I guess it turned out okay.      That’s the spirit. You’re getting better every day. Just keep working on it.      Thanks, Mum. I will. And maybe next time, I’ll take a photo that’s not upside down.

Just come round! I’ve been expecting you ages, Mavis. What kept you?      Sorry, love, I was helping out with a few things at the flat. You know how it is—somebody’s always needing a hand.      Yeah, I know the feeling. I’ve been trying to get that application form sorted for the new job. Properly got stuck on the last part.      That form always gives me the shivers. I reckon it’s written by someone who never even had to fill one themselves. All this jargon, and you’ve got to prove you’re not a criminal, or something.      I know, I know. It’s like they think we’re all potential frauds. But hey, better safe than sorry, right? I’ve been thinking about the kids in the park the other day. Proper handfuls, some of them.      I wouldn’t say that. They’re just kids. I mean, we all had our moments. Did you see that cockerel in the garden yesterday? Proper cheeky. Tried to peck at one of the baby birds in the nest.      Oh, I saw that. That bird’s got a fight on its hands. You know what I say? Let nature take its course.      Yeah, I agree. Though I do worry about them. Still, they’ll be fine.      Speaking of nature, did you hear about the 3D printer the council is planning to buy for the community center? Maybe they’ll start some kind of school project.      A 3D printer? Sounds like more of a gimmick than a real help. I’d rather have a proper set of tools.      I know, I know. But I reckon it’s a step in the right direction. At least it’s something.      Oh, look at the time! It’s nearly bedtime. I haven’t slept a wink since the kids started making that noise.      Same here. I’ve been tossing and turning all night. Must be the shabby workmanship of the new house.      I heard about that. I’m not sure if it’s the house or the neighbors. Either way, it’s giving me a headache.      Well, I’ll be here to keep you company. You never know, maybe we’ll start a new tradition—like a birthday bash.      Sounds like a plan. I’ll bring the cake.      And I’ll bring the presents. Now, don’t you go getting any ideas about moving in with us, you old devil.

So, I've been thinking a lot lately, and I think I need to talk to you about something... Well, not something too big, but it's on my mind. So, I've been meaning to ask you, how did you find the job interview for that new teaching position in Manchester? I heard it was a tough one.      Honestly, it was a bit of a nightmare. I can imagine. I was in London then, teaching a Politics module. We had a heated debate over it in class—some students were really passionate about it, others were just confused. It’s a tough time for young people. I just hope she finds her way.      Yeah, she’s strong. She’s planning to do a gap year and volunteer in Scotland. I think she’s got a real sense of purpose.      That’s great.

So, we've got the mousetrap game almost ready. I was just thinking, do you remember when we used to play this as kids? I was actually thinking, have any of you ever considered working abroad? I've heard so much about the opportunities in places like the US or Australia. So, what do you think of that rugby match last night, Oisin? I swear, the way they handled the ball was like a bunch of football players on a field.      Yeah, it was a bit strange. So, I just got a call from my sister, Sarah. She’s got a baby now, and it’s so cute, but honestly, I’m more confused than anything. Oh, moving house is a big decision. I still remember when I moved to Lincoln. It was such a big change. I had to get used to the new area, new people, and the whole rhythm of life there. So, I've been meaning to ask you, how do you even know what's going on with accents and dialects?
