So, I've been meaning to talk to you about that friend of ours, Laura. She's been snoring so loud lately, I swear she’s got her own brand of noise.      Oh, don’t even start. I’ve had to sleep with a pillow over my ears just to hear what she’s saying. It’s like she’s got a chainsaw in her throat.      That’s not even the worst part. I swear, she once woke up someone in the next flat and they called the police. Didn’t even know it was her.      Yeah, I remember that. I was in the flat next door, and I thought someone had broken in. It was just Laura. She left the door open and started talking to the ceiling like it was a friend.      Don’t get me started. I once had breakfast with her and she started snoring mid-sentence. The sausages were still on the plate, and she didn’t even notice.      Wait, you ate sausages with her? That’s the Richmond sausages, right? The ones from the market?      Yeah, the ones we always get from the bakers down the road. Mate, I don’t know how they even stay fresh.      Speaking of that, have you seen the new batch from Waterfields? They’ve been making those pastries again.      Yeah, I tried one last week. It was like eating a cloud. But I had to use a handkerchief to wipe the crumbs off my face.      I know, right? I swear those pastries are like a conspiracy. They’ve been around for years, and they still manage to taste like nothing.      You’re telling me. I once brought one to work, and my boss thought it was a weird religious offering.      Hey, I had one today. It was good, but I still had to use a handkerchief. I think I’m going to start carrying one with me.      I’ve already got a bunch of handkerchiefs on me. I wear one every day now. I’m ready for a full-time job in the fashion industry.      If you ask me, you should just start a business selling handkerchiefs. “Warrington Wipes” – it’s a name that could work.      Oh, I’d buy one. Especially if they had a logo of Laura snoring.      I’ll take that as a compliment. So, what’s next on the agenda? Should we go to the bakers and ask them what they’re doing with those pastries?

So, how was your weekend, Dad? I saw you texted me about the garden, but I never got to ask you details.      It was alright, love. Had a bit of a hectic day with the crops, but things turned out well. I actually got some good results from the new fertilizer I tried.      That's great to hear! I remember you saying you were thinking about trying something new. Did it work out?      Yeah, surprisingly, it did. I mean, I was a bit skeptical at first, but the results were decent. Still, I’ll be testing it again next week just to be sure.      That’s smart of you. I’m always learning from you, you know. You’ve got this knack for figuring things out.      Aye, well, I’ve been in this game long enough. I’ve made my share of mistakes, but I’ve also learned a lot. You're still so young, Emily, you’ve got so much time to grow.      Well, I don’t think I’ve made as many mistakes as you have, but I’m trying. Anyway, I had a good weekend too. I went to see the new exhibition at the museum. It was about British history, and it was really interesting.      Oh, really? I haven’t been to that one. I suppose it’s a bit of a drive from here, but I might have to check it out. I tend to stick to the farm most weekends, but I’d be interested in seeing something like that.      You should! It’s not too far from the village. We could go together sometime. I can even take you.      That’d be nice. I do miss a bit of culture now and then. Although, I suppose I’ve been too busy with the farm.      You don’t have to be busy all the time, Dad. You know that. You’ve got a lot to offer, but you also need to enjoy yourself.      You're right, love. I think I’ve been a bit too focused on work lately. It's good to have someone like you reminding me to take a break.      That’s what family’s for. I’m here for you, always.      And I’m here for you too. Just don’t let me overdo it with the farming, okay?      Deal. Now, let’s talk about what we’ll do this weekend.

So, I heard you mentioned you're thinking about going back to teaching? That's interesting, especially with all the changes in the education system lately. I’m still teaching English, though I've been doing a bit more language teaching online since the pandemic. It's been a bit of a shift, but I’ve enjoyed the flexibility.      It’s actually more complicated than that. I wanted to take a year off to travel and learn Spanish properly, but now I’m reconsidering. My school started offering some new programs, and they need more teachers with language skills. I’m not sure if I want to go back full-time, but it’s hard to ignore the stability, you know?      I can understand that. I still feel the same way. I left my school job last year to start teaching language courses privately, and I’ve found it rewarding. But sometimes I miss the structure of a regular school day. I even started learning French recently just for fun, though I’m not sure how far I’ll get.      That's so inspiring. I've always wanted to learn another language, but I’ve always put it off. I guess I never thought about it as a real goal until recently. My daughter started learning Spanish in nursery, and it's made me realize how important it is. Maybe I should take it more seriously.      That’s a great point. I’ve been telling my students that learning a language isn’t just about grammar and vocabulary—it’s about connecting with other cultures. My mom always said, “If you can read a book in another language, you can understand people better.” It’s a bit cliché, but it’s true.      I love that. I’ve been thinking about taking a course myself. But honestly, with my daughter and all the other responsibilities, I don’t know where I’d fit it in. You're lucky you can do it alongside your job. I feel like I’m always juggling too much.      You’re not alone. I’ve got a student who’s pregnant, and we’ve been chatting about the whole baby experience. I remember being so clueless when I was first pregnant. It’s one thing to teach language, but it's another to navigate the whole parenting journey.      I know. I think I’m more nervous about the baby than I am about teaching.

Well, I've just been out in the garden, and I noticed one of the bird feeders has gone missing again. I'm starting to think it's the magpies. They've been getting bolder these days.      Aye, I've seen them hanging around more. They’re not the same as they used to be. But I reckon if you put up a better feeder, they might just leave it alone. I remember when we first got the one with the sunflower seeds, it was a real haven for the birds.      I still keep the old one out, even though it's not working so well. I love watching the birds, especially the sparrows. They come in the morning, just before the sun rises. It’s like a little orchestra of chirping.      That’s the charm of it, isn’t it? I used to have a breakfast routine with the birds. I’d sit with a cup of tea and a slice of cake, and they’d all come to feed. It was peaceful, almost like a ritual.      I used to do that too. I even had a little sign to let the birds know I was there. But lately, I’ve been spending more time pacing in the garden. You know, thinking about old times. Still, I can’t help but miss the company of the birds.      I’ve started making little bird cakes, like you used to make, Speaker_1. I think they’re a hit. Just a simple sponge with some seeds on top. I put them out each morning, and they’re always gone by midday.      That’s a nice idea. I’ve always thought bird feeders could double as a kind of puppet theater. You know, you could string up some strings and make them move like puppets. Though I’m not sure the birds would appreciate the show.      Haha, I reckon they’d think it’s a game. You know how they like to play with strings and sticks. Maybe we could make a little puppet out of wood and hang it near the feeder. It might keep them entertained.      I think that’s a great idea. It could be a way to go out of the house and do something creative. I’ve been feeling a bit stuck in the house lately, with all the weather being so unpredictable.      I know what you mean. Being retired and not working has its downsides, but there’s also a lot to be said for having time to think and do things that matter.

So, I've been meaning to ask you, how do you say “one” in Turkish? I saw a sign in the market the other day, and I thought I’d try to learn a few words.      Ah, that’s a good idea. I learned a bit when I was in Istanbul a few years back. “Bir” is “one,” and “iki” is “two.” But I think it's best to just pick up a few phrases and go with it. You'll be surprised how people respond to a little effort.      I suppose so. It’s been a while since I’ve been to Turkey, but I remember the food was amazing. Speaking of which, I’ve been craving some local specialties here. Do you know where I could find the best kebabs in Nicosia?      Oh, you’re in for a treat. Down by the market, there’s a place called  Yusuf’s —they have the best lamb skewers. And don’t miss the  mercimek çorbası —it’s a lentil soup I can never get enough of.      Thanks, I’ll have to try that. By the way, have you noticed how many people here have dogs? I’ve seen more than a few walking around with them, and some even have little flags on their collars.      You’re not the only one. Our neighbor, Mrs. Patel, has two dogs. She’s a bit of a breeder, I think. But the thing is, she lost her husband last year. That’s where the flags come in—each one represents a family member. It’s a lovely gesture, though it’s a bit sad.      That’s touching. I’ve lost a few people in the past few years, and it’s hard to keep up with the changes. I’ve started using hearing aids, actually. They’re a bit awkward, but they’ve made a world of difference.      That’s great to hear. I know how frustrating it can be. I’ve been thinking about getting some myself. My wife keeps saying I’m getting too quiet.      Well, you’ve got to keep your voice strong. Speaking of which, I’ve been trying to teach my niece how to count in Turkish. She’s six, so it’s not too late.      That’s adorable. Just like I did with my son. I remember when he first asked, “What’s this?” and I had to go through the whole alphabet with him.

So, I've been thinking about the house a lot lately. I know it's not the most modern, but I feel like we could do a few things to make it feel more like  our  place. Maybe we could redo the kitchen? That would be a big change, but it would make a real difference.      That’s a good point, actually. I agree that the kitchen could use some love. But I’m not too sure about the cost. You know how things can add up so quickly. Maybe we could start small and see how we go.      I’ve been thinking about that too. I’ve got a few ideas for the garden as well. You know, the turkey enclosure is getting a bit run-down. I could do some work on the fences and maybe add a few more trees. If we do that, it might make the whole place feel more like a home, not just a house.      That sounds perfect. I was actually thinking about Christmas presents too. I was going to get everyone something special, but I was worried about the budget. Do you think we could get the kids some new bikes? They’ve been asking for ages, and I think they’d really appreciate it.      Bikes are a good idea. But maybe we should split the cost. I know you’ve been saving up for the kitchen, and I’m still getting used to the budget after being in education for so long. I’d hate for either of us to feel the strain.      That’s fair. I had the same problem when I started my own business. I had to be really careful with every penny. But I did manage to save up for the turkeys, so I’m not too bad. Maybe we can all chip in a little.      Yeah, that could work. I think it’s important that we all contribute. It makes it feel more like a team effort. Speaking of which, have you all heard about the rugby match next month? The local team is going to play in the championship.      Oh, I can’t wait! I’ve been trying to get back into it after a few years. It’s a great way to stay in shape and get some fresh air. I think I’ll be heading down with some of the other teachers.      I might try to go too.

So, I was just watching Jeremy Kyle the other day, and it was  so  intense. I mean, I’ve seen some wild stuff on that show, but this one had me on edge.      Yeah, I remember that. The guy on the show was  so  defensive. I didn’t know he had a catfish. What’s a catfish, even?      Oh, you know, like someone pretending to be someone else online? They set up a whole fake identity to mess with people. It’s like,  why even do that?       Exactly! And this guy was supposedly a guy, but he was actually a woman. And she was talking to this guy who thought he was her ex. It was so funny.      I mean, I get it. People are weird, but I don’t know, it’s just so  unreal . I mean, why not just tell the truth? It’s not like it’s the end of the world.      I guess it’s more about the thrill, though. Like,  how far can I go before someone catches me?  But come on, I wouldn’t do that. I mean, I’m not a big fan of lies.      Same here. I mean, I’ve never even thought about doing anything like that. But I can see why people might get into it. It’s kind of like a game, right? You’re trying to outwit someone.      Yeah, but it’s not just a game. People get hurt. I mean, I’ve seen some stories where people end up losing trust in their relationships because of catfishing. It’s not just for fun.      That’s true. I guess it’s a bit like those reality shows, but more real. You can’t just edit out the drama. It’s all there, and it’s so messy.      Yeah, it’s like  The Jeremy Kyle Show —just the drama, no filter. But I still can’t get over that catfish episode. I mean, how did they even manage to pull it off?      I don’t know, but I’m guessing it was a lot of acting. And I don’t think they expected the guy to get so worked up.      I think that’s the whole point. You’re trying to mess with someone, and then they take it seriously. It’s like,  what’s the point of it all?       I don’t know, but I think it’s just a reminder that people can be really dramatic.

So, I was just telling my mum about the time I tried to order a croissant in Paris and ended up speaking German instead of French. I think I confused the waiter so much he just gave me the wrong thing and left.      Oh, I remember that sort of thing. I used to travel a lot before I settled in England. You know, I’ve been to Paris several times, but every time I go, I still mix up the French and German. My grandfather was German, so maybe it's just in my blood.      Yeah, but I guess it's also because I studied German at university. I found it easier than French, honestly. My lectures were all in German, and I got so used to it. I even wrote my thesis in it, which was a bit of a nightmare.      Oh, you’re a graduate, aren’t you? I used to be a classics student too. I studied Latin and Greek in my youth, and it’s amazing how that still helps with languages. It’s like bones—you can’t really forget them.      That’s true. I’ve always been fascinated by languages, even as a kid. I used to play with my little brother, and we’d make up our own language. I guess it was my version of a dream—like, if the world was perfect, we’d all speak the same thing. But then again, I’m not the only one. I’ve heard you speak Italian too, haven’t you?      Yes, I do. I grew up in Vienna, but my family is from Italy. My grandmother used to speak Italian, and I picked it up from her. It’s strange, living in England and still speaking Italian. I feel like I’m always between two worlds.      That must be amazing. I wish I had a language like that. I mean, I can speak English, German, and a bit of French. But I never got the chance to learn Italian. Maybe I should try. I could always visit Italy one day.      You should. I’ve been there a few times, and it’s just breathtaking. The food, the history, the people. I think you’d really go there and feel right at home.      I’d love to. Maybe when I finish my studies, I’ll take a trip. I’ve been meaning to go to Italy for ages, but I’ve always been too busy with uni and computer problems.

Did you see the driver who just cut me off on the motorway? He was doing like 70 mph in the left lane, and I had to swerve to avoid him! It’s like he’s trying to race the traffic lights!      I saw that too. I swear, some people think they’re on a track instead of a road. I’ve had more accidents with drivers like that than with actual potholes. You know what’s worse? When it rains and you can’t see a thing. Didn’t you get stuck in that traffic jam on the M20 last week?      Yeah, that was a nightmare. I had to wait for over an hour. I left work early just to get there on time, and I still missed the meeting. The lights turned red every 30 seconds, and no one would move. I nearly had a panic attack.      Oh, I’d be the first to panic! I remember when I was driving to my uni exams, and I got stuck in traffic because of a broken-down lorry. I had to call my mum and tell her I was going to be late. She said, “Don’t worry, it’s only a little exam.” I said, “It’s not a little exam, it’s my whole future!”      You’re not the only one who’s had that kind of anxiety. I used to drive to work every day and get so stressed. That’s why I retired early. I can’t handle the pressure anymore.      I get it. I’ve been working as a care assistant for years, and I’m always worried about being late. But the thing is, I can’t afford to take days off. My sister is the one who takes the days off. She said she’s going to take a holiday for the first time in years. I told her, “You should have done that a long time ago!”      I hear you. I’m going on a trip to France next month. I’m going to take a week off work. I’ve been saving up for ages. I just need to book the flights and the accommodation.      That sounds good. But I still can’t get over the thought of using a Sat Nav. I always end up somewhere weird. I remember once I followed a Sat Nav to a town called Mantiques, and it turned out to be a fictional place.

I've been thinking a lot lately, you know. I've had a few years of being out of work and it's been a tough road. You ever feel like you're just waiting for something to happen, but nothing does? Oh, I know what you mean. I've been in the same boat for a while now. I used to be a childminder, you know, but after the last few years, things just dried up. It's like the world moved on and left us behind. Yeah, and it's not like we're young anymore. I keep telling myself I'll get back to work, but who's going to hire a man in his seventies? Still, I can't just sit around doing nothing all day. It's hard, isn't it? You feel useless, like you're not contributing to anything. I used to look after kids and feel like I was making a difference. Now I just sit here, watching the telly and waiting for the phone to ring. I've been thinking about getting back into some kind of work, maybe something part-time. I’ve got the skills, you know. I did have a job in the post office for years. Maybe I could do something like that again. That's a good idea. Maybe you could try looking into local job centres or something. I’ve heard they have some programmes for people like us. Maybe something with the council or the community centre. I was thinking about that. But I’m not sure how to approach it. I mean, I haven’t done this in years. It's like starting from scratch again. You can do it, you know. I've been thinking about it too. Maybe we can help each other. I can take you to the job centre, and we can go through everything together. It might be easier that way. That sounds like a plan. I'd feel better knowing I’m not on my own. You've always been there for me, even when I felt like I was falling apart. I'm here for you, always. And besides, I think it's time we both took a step back and looked forward. You know, it's never too late to try something new. You're right. Maybe I should start small. Just go and see what's out there.

So, I was just thinking about that old band we used to listen to when we were in uni—The Smiths. Remember how we used to argue about whether Morrissey was a genius or just a drama queen?      Oh, I remember. You were all for him, and I was like, 'He just sounds like he's having a meltdown on a Tuesday.' But now I actually think he had a lot of depth. Still, I can't get over that voice of his—like a broken record.      Yeah, I still think he had some real talent. But I can’t stand the new stuff they’re putting out. It feels like they’re trying too hard to be alternative. I miss the raw energy of the old days.      I hear you. I’ve been thinking about starting a garden again. The last time I tried, it was a disaster. I ended up with more weeds than vegetables. But I remember how much you loved gardening when we first moved in. You were always out there with your trowel and your clipboard.      I did love it, but life got in the way. I mean, who has time to grow tomatoes when you’re managing a research team and trying to figure out the meaning of life? But maybe it’s time to get back to it. I’ve been meaning to plant some herbs. I could use a little more green around the house.      That sounds good. I’ve been reading up on gardening tips. I think I’m going to start with some herbs too. Maybe even a few flowers. I remember your grandmother used to have the most beautiful garden. She always said the best vegetables grow when you treat them like people.      She did say that. And she wasn’t wrong. I think she had a way of talking to her plants like they were her best friends. I remember once she said, 'The tomatoes are just trying to grow, just like we all are. You’ve got to give them time.'      Yeah, and you were the one who kept trying to feed them sugar water. I told you that would make them sick.      Oh, don’t bring that up! I was just trying to be a good gardener. And what about the weather? It’s been so strange lately. One day it’s sunny, the next it’s pouring with rain.

So, I was just thinking about how things have changed since I was a student. I remember when we were all worrying about university fees and whether we’d even be able to afford a degree. Now, with the cost of living rising and the job market so uncertain, it feels like everyone’s in a different boat.      I know, it’s wild. I’m still in that boat, honestly. I’ve been a PhD student for nearly three years now, and every time I think I’ve got it figured out, something new comes along. I mean, the funding situation is so unpredictable. One week you’re getting a grant, the next you’re scrambling to find a part-time job just to keep your head above water.      I remember you saying something like that last week. You were talking about how you had to take a casual job in a café just to cover your rent. How’s that working out for you?      Honestly, it’s been a rollercoaster. The café is okay, but the hours are inconsistent. And I still feel like I’m not making progress with my research. Sometimes I think I’d rather be working in a proper job, even if it’s not in my field, just to have some stability. But then I remember why I started this PhD in the first place – I want to make a real contribution.      I get that. I was in a similar place when I started my research management job. I had to quit my previous role because it was just too unstable. But looking back, it was the right move. I mean, I’m out of university, but I still have the anxiety of being ‘between jobs’ all the time. You know, the feeling that you’re always searching for the next step, even when you’re not sure what it is.      That sounds like me. I even joked the other day that I should just go work for the government. At least then I’d have a guaranteed income and benefits. But the thought of working in a bureaucratic system makes me feel like I’m giving up on my ambitions.      I know what you mean. It’s like we’re all stuck in this limbo between academic and professional life. Still, I think it’s better than unemployment. At least you’re still moving forward, even if it’s not in the direction you thought.

Okay, so I was thinking—what if we made a book about our family? Like, a kids’ book that tells our family story. I mean, it could have pictures of all of us, and little stories about how we met or what we like to do.      That’s a nice idea, but I’m not sure about the pictures. I mean, I don’t have a camera, and I’m not sure where we’d get the photos. But maybe we could use some old photos from the past? Like the ones my mum used to take when we were kids.      Oh, I’ve got some old photos, actually. I kept them all in a box in my attic. I could bring them down. And if you want, I can help you write the stories too. I used to teach kids, so I know how to make it simple and engaging for children.      That’d be great! I think it could help the kids understand where we come from. You know, the stories about why we have different family styles. Like, why you and my dad separated, and how I have two different stepfathers.      Yeah, that’s something I’ve never really talked about in detail. I mean, I know the kids know a bit, but not the full story. Maybe this book could help us all understand each other better.      I think that’s a good point. Family is about connection, even when things get complicated. Like my own family—my brother moved to Scotland years ago, and we don’t see each other as much as we used to. But I still feel close to him.      That’s true. I feel like my family is more like a mix of different pieces. My mum is from Bristol, and my dad is from London, and now I’m living in Ireland. It’s a bit confusing at times, but I think it makes us unique.      Exactly. And I think the book could help the kids see that. Like, maybe they can see how different family structures work. Some people have two parents, others have one parent, and some have step-parents. It’s all valid.      I agree. It’s not about how many parents you have—it’s about who loves you. And I think this book could be a way to show that. It could also include a family tree, like the one I made when I was a teacher.

So, I’ve been thinking about that thing we talked about last week — you know, the whole shaving thing? I’ve been trying to figure out if I should actually start shaving my legs. I mean, I’ve always left them natural, but now I’m like, maybe it’s time to grow up a bit?      Oh, grow up? You’re barely out of sixth form! I mean, I get it — some people think it’s a rite of passage. But honestly, I don’t see the point. It’s just extra work. You get razor burns, ingrown hairs, and then you’re left with this dumb, awkward look. I’d rather just keep them as they are.      Well, I guess I’m not the only one who’s confused. I asked my sister, and she said she’d definitely do it if she were in a relationship. But I’m not in a relationship — yet — and I’m not sure if I want to follow the “norm.” Also, I’ve heard that some girls like to have it, and others don’t. It’s really about personal choice, right?      Yeah, totally. I think it’s a personal thing. But honestly, I’d rather just go with what feels natural. I mean, I’ve got a bit of body hair on my arms and legs, and I don’t mind it. It’s not like it’s a big deal. Plus, I don’t want someone to think I’m trying too hard to fit in. It’s one thing to do it for a partner, but it’s another to do it just because everyone else is.      You’re right about that. I think I’m just trying to figure out what makes me comfortable. I mean, I’ve been rolling with the natural look for a while now, but I’ve seen so many girls go the other way. I feel like it’s like a trend. Like, if you don’t do it, you’re not  cool  or something. I mean, I don’t want to be cool — I just want to be me.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? You don’t want to change yourself for anyone else. I mean, I’ve seen so many people get caught up in trying to look a certain way, and it ends up making them feel worse. You’re not defined by your body hair, or your style, or anything like that.

So, I was just thinking—what's the first thing that comes to mind when you think of the alphabet? Like, what's the first letter you associate with something important in your life?      Hmm, that’s a good question. For me, it’s “R.” Because I think of my dad, who always told me, “R is for resilience.” He was into boxing, you know. Used to take me to the gym when I was a kid.      Oh, boxing! I’ve got a friend who’s into it too. He says it’s not just about strength—it’s about discipline. But I’ve never been the type to get into a ring. Though I do like a good pint.      Right, I get that. You know, I used to drink a lot when I was younger. Before I started my PhD, I’d get down to the pub every night. But now, I only drink on weekends, and even then, it’s just a couple of pints.      That’s wise. I’ve had my fair share of nights where I thought, “I’ll just have one more,” and then it turned into a whole evening. But I’ve learned to set limits. Though I still think the pub scene is one of the best places to meet people.      Absolutely. And that’s what I love about places like this in Cambridge. You get all sorts of people in here. From students to locals, everyone’s got a story. It’s amazing how much you can learn just by listening.      Speaking of stories, I remember hearing about a guy who used to do some drugs back in the day. He said it was all about the rush. But I’ve never been into that. I think the only high I’ve ever had was when I passed my postgrad exams.      Yeah, I can relate. I remember when I first started my PhD, I was stressed out, and I tried some things to cope. But I realized it wasn’t helping. Now I just rely on my support network—my friends, my family.      That’s something. You know, I’ve also been thinking about racism in football. It’s still a problem, even here in Cambridge. I’ve seen some really ugly stuff at matches, and it’s sad.      Totally. I’ve had friends who’ve been kicked out of stadiums for just being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

So, I've been thinking about the old mill in Cheltenham. We need to get that listed, don’t you think? It’s got so much character, and it’s been standing there for over two hundred years.      I agree, but the problem is the funding. The council’s been hesitant to fund any major restoration. I think we need to approach them with a solid business plan. You know, one that shows how the project will bring in revenue and preserve the local heritage.      I was just talking to a friend of mine who’s a fundraiser. She suggested we look into European grants—those Horizon Europe funds. They’ve been giving out money for heritage projects across the UK. It’s worth applying for, especially if we can tie the project to tourism.      That’s a good point. But I’m not sure how to structure the bid. I remember when I helped a chapel in Hertfordshire get funding, the key was showing that the project would not only be environmentally sustainable but also create jobs. It helped them get the grant.      Exactly! We need to make sure the proposal highlights both the historical and economic value. Also, I’ve been reading about using crowdfunding platforms. Maybe we can start a campaign to raise some initial funds. It builds community support and shows the project is viable.      I like that idea. But I’m still worried about the regulatory side. Historic buildings have strict rules about what you can alter. I read somewhere that if you don’t follow the guidelines, you could lose your grant.      True, but I think we can work with a heritage consultant. I know someone who does that. They can help us navigate the regulations and ensure we’re compliant. It might even be easier to get the council on board if we have that kind of support.      That sounds like a plan. I’ll reach out to the consultant tomorrow. But I think we should also start drafting the proposal. The earlier we get it out, the better. I’ll draft the business plan, and you can help with the funding section.      Deal. I’ll bring my notes from the meeting with the European funding body. I think we can make this work.      Alright, let’s get started. This might be the most exciting project we’ve had in years.      I couldn’t agree more.

You know, I’ve been thinking about that linguistics paper we were reading last week. The one about dialectal variations in the UK? It’s fascinating how regional accents can reflect historical migration patterns.      Yeah, it was interesting how they linked the Midlands accent to the Norman Conquest and the subsequent mixing of French and English. But don’t you think there’s more to it? I mean, isn’t it also about social class and education?      Absolutely. I was just arguing with my colleague about that. Some people think it’s mostly about geography, but I believe socio-economic factors play a huge role too. Take my hometown, Sunderland. You’ve got a strong working-class accent, but there are also educated professionals who speak with a more refined tone. It’s like a blend of both.      I can see that. I grew up in Birmingham, and the accent there is pretty distinct. But I’ve noticed that the younger generation is starting to shift. I think it’s because of media and education—people are exposed to different ways of speaking.      Exactly. I’ve been researching this for my postgrad work. It’s got to do with how language evolves. Plus, the internet has made it easier for people to pick up different accents and styles.      You’re not the only one doing that. I’ve been working on my PhD for over a year now, and I’ve been recording dialects in different regions for my study. It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster, but it’s worth it.      That’s impressive. I’m still trying to keep up with my research projects. But I think it’s easier now with the tools we have. Still, I miss the days when I could just go out and collect data in the field.      You know, I was thinking about taking a break and going on holiday. You ever think about going somewhere to study dialects? Maybe to the Scottish Highlands? There’s a lot of variation there, and the scenery is amazing.      That sounds perfect. I’ve always wanted to go there. It’s not just the language—it’s the culture, the history, the food. You could write a thesis just on your holiday.      Yeah, I’m sure I could. But I might just end up writing a blog instead.      You’d be surprised how much you can learn from a holiday.

Okay, I've got to talk to the kids about the school dinner money. I know they’re supposed to bring £2 each week for lunch, but I don’t want them to feel like they’re being charged for every meal.      Mum, can I have a bit more cheese? I like it with my crackers.      I wanted to eat the strawberry jam too. It’s my favorite.      You both know we’ve got to stick to the budget. The school dinners are pretty good, but sometimes the kids say they don’t like the food. Have you tried the new ones?      I tried the chicken nuggets last week, but they were too salty. I would have preferred the spaghetti.      I thought the spaghetti was good. But then the chef made a mistake and gave me carrots instead of pasta.      Oh no, that sounds messy. I’ll have to talk to the school about that. But the main thing is, we need to make sure the kids have enough money for lunch every day. I know the school is organizing a tennis tournament next week, and I don’t want them to be hungry during the games.      Can we have a pizza day? I really like pizza.      Pizza is fine, but it’s not always on the menu. We might need to save up for a special day. How about we plan for a pizza day next Friday?      That’s a good idea! I can ask my friends if they want to come over too.      That’s great. But remember, you can only bring one friend at a time. And if you want pizza, you’ll need to bring your own money.      What if I don’t have enough money?      Then we can talk about it. I know you’ve been saving up, but if you need help, I’m here. Also, I overheard the school is having a clown visit next week. I think it’s related to the tennis tournament.      Clowns? Are they going to be in the gym?      I don’t know the details yet, but I imagine they’ll be doing some fun activities. Maybe even some games. It could be a great way to relieve stress after the tournament.      I think clowns are cool. I’ve seen them at the circus before.      Yeah, I remember going to the circus when I was your age. It always made me feel so excited.

So, did you see that film we went to last night? I thought it was pretty good, but I got a bit lost in the middle. It felt like it was trying to be serious, but the dialogue just wasn’t clicking.      I agree. It was a bit of a mess. I liked the idea of the film, but the way it was presented—like they were trying too hard to be profound. I think they lost the audience.      You know, I actually had a similar thought. It reminded me of that debate in Cambridge last week about how to teach history. They were arguing whether to focus more on narrative or analysis. I think that film was trying to do both, but it failed at both.      Yeah, I heard about that debate too. I think the whole education system is stuck in this cycle. On one hand, we’re supposed to be preparing kids for the real world, but on the other hand, we’re still teaching history like it’s a series of facts to memorize.      Exactly. And it’s not just history. I mean, the national curriculum in England is constantly changing. One year it’s one thing, and the next year it’s something else. I got out of school 50 years ago, and I can still remember the curriculum better than some of the kids I see now.      It’s a bit frustrating, isn’t it? I mean, someone with my education—postgrad in business—can still find it hard to navigate the system. I had to do a lot of self-teaching and industry experience to make sense of it all.      That’s a good point. I think the real issue is the gap between education and the real world. You get all this academic knowledge, but if you don’t have practical experience, you’re not really prepared for the workforce.      And with the current state of the economy, you can’t afford to be unprepared. You’ve got to have the right skills, and that doesn’t always come from sitting in a classroom. I think the government’s pushing for more internships and work experience, but I’m not sure how effective that is.      It’s a start, but I think the focus should be on making higher education more relevant. If you’re going to spend six years studying, it should have a clear link to the industries you want to enter.

Well, I've been thinking about the war again, you know. It's strange how time slips away, but the memories stay. I remember the days when the air raids were a constant thing. Back in Costessey, we'd all gather in the basement of the church, like the place was a sanctuary.      Oh, I remember that too. My gran used to tell me stories about how the men from Harrow would come back after the war, changed but still the same. She said it was like they’d been through a fire and came out the other side.      I was a bit too young to be involved in the war myself, but I can recall the impact it had on our families. My father was a military officer, and I grew up hearing the tales of bravery, sacrifice, and loss. The war shaped so many lives, even for those who didn’t fight on the front lines.      That's true. The war’s legacy is still felt today, even in the way we think about national unity and community. It’s interesting how the things we learned from that time still influence our attitudes toward conflict and cooperation.      Yeah, and the war wasn’t just about men risking their lives. It was about the way people looked out for each other. I still remember the night the bombs fell, and how we all held hands in the basement, just trying to stay calm. It was a time when fear and hope walked hand in hand.      I think that’s what makes those memories so powerful. It wasn’t just about the fear; it was about the resilience. Even in the darkest times, people found ways to make the best of things. My mum always said that the real heroes were the ones who stayed behind and kept the family going.      That’s a beautiful thought. Maybe that’s why I found myself drawn to the idea of education and community work. There's something about helping others to recover and rebuild that echoes the spirit of those times.      I agree. The values we learned then—like solidarity, duty, and compassion—are still relevant today. They just take different forms depending on the era. Still, I think they’re the foundation of the kind of society we want to build.      And don’t forget the weather. It plays a part in all of this, doesn’t it?

So, we've got a few things to sort out before we move, right? I think it's time we actually start packing. I’ve been meaning to talk about it with you, but I’ve been busy with the students and all that.      Yeah, I was thinking the same thing. I’ve been trying to figure out the logistics of moving everything. I’ve got that storage unit in Milton Keynes, but I’m not sure if I should pay for the extra space. It might not be worth it.      Wait, when are we actually moving? You said you wanted to finalize the date by the end of the month, right?      Yes, the Saturday after next. I’ve already booked the removal van. They’re coming to pick up the things from Mum’s and deliver them to the new place. It’s all set, really.      That’s good. I just hope everything goes smoothly. I’ve been trying to finish up some of the paperwork for the mortgage. I’m not sure how much of it I can do without being there in person.      You’ve got to remember, you’re not the only one who’s been working on it. I’ve been helping you with the forms, and I know you’ve been struggling with the financial side of it. It’s not easy, but we’ll get through it.      You’re right. It’s just frustrating because I feel like I’m still dealing with everything from the past. That’s why I’ve been thinking about getting the mortgage sorted early. I don’t want to be stuck in this house longer than necessary.      That makes sense. I know it’s been hard on you, especially with what happened last year. You were sick for so long, and it really took a toll on the whole family.      Yeah, I still feel the effects sometimes. But I’m getting better. I think I’m ready to move on.      That’s good to hear. Let’s make sure we take some time to enjoy the last few days here. I’ve got a few things I want to do with the kids before we leave. Maybe go to the cinema? There’s that new movie about the old days—something about the 70s.      That sounds like a good idea. I’ve been meaning to catch that. We can take the kids to the cinema and then have dinner at that new Italian place near the station.

Okay, I've got the list of people coming for the birthday dinner. Let me just check the seating plan again. I don’t want anyone sitting next to someone they don’t get along with.      You’re overcomplicating it! It’s just a dinner for your mum. She’s got a few friends coming, and the rest are family. Why not just put everyone around the table? A few people might not know each other, but it’s not like they’re going to start a fight.      I know, but it’s her birthday. I don’t want to seem like I’m treating it like a formal event. But I do want to make sure the seating feels warm and comfortable. I’ve already sketched out a basic plan. Let me see... Dad and his sister can be on one side, the cousins on the other, and then the guests at the end.      That sounds good. But wait, what’s the menu again? You mentioned you were looking for a recipe from the Great British Bake Off. I saw one for a lemon drizzle cake that’s super moist. I could make that.      Yes, that sounds perfect. I was also thinking of having some fish, like salmon. I saw a recipe that uses a mix of herbs, and I think it’s going to be tasty. But I need to buy the fish tomorrow. Should I pick it up from the fishmonger, or should I just get it online?      Why not just buy it online? You can get it delivered, and it’ll be fresh. But wait, did you check the candles? You said you wanted to do something special for the cake. I picked up some lit candles, but I’m not sure if they’re the right size.      Yes, the ones that have the little ‘Happy Birthday’ on them. I think they’re going to be perfect. Oh, and I was going to rearrange the cupboards in the kitchen for more storage space. I’ve got some photos of how I want to organize them.      That’s a good idea. I’ve been meaning to do that too. And by the way, your mum mentioned she’s been having some trouble with her memory lately. Maybe we should make sure the seating is close to the food so she doesn’t get lost or confused.      You’re right.

So, I’ve been trying to get my wisdom teeth out for ages, but I keep putting it off. I mean, I’m not exactly  dying  or anything, but I can’t even chew properly anymore. My mouth is like a war zone.      Ugh, I know, right? I’ve got the same thing. I keep telling myself I’ll just wait until the summer, but I’m so tired of seeing those bumps in my mouth. Plus, my parents are like, “You need to get them done,” but I don’t wanna spend all that money. What’s the point?      Yeah, I’ve been trying to save up, but I’m living with my parents and I’m not exactly rolling in cash. I mean, I’m a student, not a millionaire. But I’m also not about to wait until I’m 40 and then suddenly have a  full  set of wisdom teeth. It’s like,  why?       I know, I know. It’s just one of those things—like, you don’t really think about it until it starts hurting. I’ve got a hole in my tooth from a cavity, and it’s getting worse. I was going to go to the dentist this week, but I just feel so lazy. I’ve been staying up too late studying and not taking care of myself.      I can relate. I’ve been so distracted with uni work that I haven’t even thought about my dental health. But seriously, I think I need to make a move. I mean, I can’t keep being like this. I’ve got a new flat coming up in September, and I don’t want to move into a place with holes in the walls and a bad tooth.      Yeah, it’s a bit of both. I’m moving out for the first time, too. My parents are going to be moving house, so the whole family is getting a bit of a shuffle. I’m really excited, but I’m also worried about the move. I mean, how do you even start with a new place?      I know, it’s overwhelming. But I think once you get into the rhythm of it, it’s not that bad. I mean, I’m moving in with my partner, so we’re figuring it out together. It’s like starting a new chapter. Although I still have to get my wisdom teeth done first.

Okay, so I was thinking about the Chinese New Year. I’ve been meaning to do something special for it, and I thought maybe we could do some random acts of kindness. I've heard that people in some countries do things like giving charity or helping out strangers as a way to celebrate the new year.      That sounds cool! But what kind of acts of kindness can we do? I mean, I love giving things to people, but I don’t have much money.      I can help with that. My mom said we can use the Chess and Draughts pieces like money. Like, we can make little "coins" out of them and then give them to someone who needs it.      Oh, that’s a clever idea! I like the way you think, Speaker_3. But I was also thinking of making lactose-free cakes and cookies. I’ve been experimenting with recipes lately. Maybe we can give some to the neighbors or the local community center?      That’s a great idea! I could help with the baking. I love making things, even if I’m just in primary school.      Can we color the cookies? I’ve seen videos where people put food coloring on them. My friend Mateo showed me how to make rainbow cookies.      Absolutely! It would be a nice touch. And if we do this for Chinese New Year, we could even label the cookies with little red envelopes and say “Happy New Year” in Chinese. I can look up some basic phrases.      I want to die my hair different colors too, like the colors in the cookies! My friend Lily does that, and it looks amazing.      That’s fun, but I think we should be careful. Dyeing your hair can be tricky. Maybe we can try it after the cookies are done.      What if we use the wooden pieces from the Chess set as little money to buy hair dye? That way, we’re using our "coins" for something meaningful.      That’s such a creative way to think about it. I love how you’re connecting all these ideas. Let’s map out a plan: tomorrow, we can gather the ingredients for the cakes, and then on Friday we can bake them. Then on Saturday, we’ll hand them out to the neighbors and maybe even the postman.      I can help with everything! I just need to bring my coloring supplies.

So, I was just telling my friend about the time I got into a car accident... Well, not  me , but my cousin. She was driving with her friend, and they were both doing 70 on a country road, and—  poof  —a seagull flew out of nowhere, and  biff ! They swerved, and the car ended up on its side. A total mess.      Oh no, that’s something. I can imagine the chaos. But seagulls in the car? That’s not something I’d expect.      I know, right? It was hilarious, but terrifying. My cousin had a scar on her forehead from the impact. She says it’s like a little crown now.      Oh, that’s a strange way to look at it. I suppose it’s a reminder of something... but in a funny way.      Yeah, she hides it with her hair most of the time. But I think she’s taking it as a badge of honor. Speaking of scars, I got one on my arm from that time I tried to dye my hair blue.      That’s a classic. I had a friend who tried to dye her hair green, and it looked like something out of  Alice in Wonderland .      That’s funny! I remember reading  Alice in Wonderland  when I was younger. It was one of those books that made me wonder if the world was just a dream.      It’s a bit of a surreal story, isn’t it? I’ve always thought it was about growing up and dealing with the absurdity of life.      I guess that’s why I like reading so much. It’s like escaping into another world. I just finished a play for school, and it was about a girl who discovers she can talk to animals.      That sounds amazing. I loved theatre when I was younger. I used to act in school plays. Though I’m not sure I’d ever be brave enough to audition again.      You should try it! It’s so much fun. And I’ve been thinking about getting a costume for Halloween. Maybe something like a pirate or a vampire.      That sounds exciting. I’ve been thinking about getting a new outfit too. I’ve been on the internet a lot lately, trying to find the perfect one.      Oh, you’re into the internet? I used to spend all my time on it, but now I prefer reading.

Well, I've been thinking about the protest group in our area again. They’re fighting against the wind turbine plans, and it's all getting pretty heated. I remember last night, when we met with the solar panel group, they seemed really informed, but they were still struggling with the same issues — the local council, the energy companies, and the government.      Yes, it's a tough fight. I was with them last night too. I got the feeling they're not just up against the local committee — they're up against the whole system. The council seems to be leaning heavily on the energy companies, but I don't think they're doing it for the right reasons. They’re getting money from the companies, of course, and that’s influencing their decisions.      Exactly. I've seen this pattern before. I used to work in a company that dealt with government contracts and grants. It's all about funding. The government gives billions to energy companies in subsidies, but when it comes to research — especially on alternative energy storage — the budget is way smaller. That’s a problem. You can’t have wind turbines or solar panels if you can’t store the energy properly.      That's true. I've been reading about it. The storage issue is the big one. Without reliable storage, you can’t really rely on renewable energy sources. It’s like the old saying — don’t put all your eggs in one basket. But the government keeps putting all the eggs in the energy companies’ basket.      And it's not just about the storage. It’s about the tactics too. These protest groups need to be well-informed and strategic. We can’t just rely on shouting about it. We need to research the planning appeal process, find loopholes, and maybe even get some legal support. The local planners are barely informed, and the energy companies are pulling strings behind the scenes.      And then there’s the Scottish referendum. It's only two weeks away. If the people there vote to leave, it could shift the whole political landscape. The energy companies might not be as powerful in Scotland if they lose their grip on the market. But I don’t think the government is going to let that happen easily.      That's the thing — it's about power. If we can educate the public, if we can make people understand the long-term benefits of sustainable energy, maybe we can change the system.

Well, I've been meaning to talk to you about that driving thing. You know, you've been asking about taking the test for ages. I think it's about time you got your license.      Thanks, Dad, I know. It's just that I haven’t had much time to practice. Work’s been keeping me pretty busy lately. Plus, I’m still trying to get a feel for the car.      I remember when I learned. It was a bit of a nightmare at first. I used to get so flustered when the traffic lights changed. But once you get the hang of it, it’s not so bad.      Yes, it’s all about confidence, love. You can’t let the pressure get to you. I had a friend, old Bill, who took the test three times before he got it. But he was determined.      I’m not sure I’m ready for that. What about insurance? I heard it’s pretty expensive for a new driver.      Oh, yes, it can be. But I think if you take a driving course first, it might help. Some insurance companies offer better rates for people who've done that.      That’s a good point. I know a guy who took a course and got his insurance down by quite a bit. You might want to look into that.      Thanks for the tip. I’ll check that out. Also, what are your plans for the week? You mentioned you were thinking about going away.      Well, I was thinking of going up to the Lake District. It’s been a while since we went, and the weather’s looking decent. We could take the car, of course.      That sounds lovely. I’d like to go with you. It’s been ages since we had a proper holiday.      We can talk about it more next week. You know, your mum and I are looking to take a trip to Spain next year. We’ve been saving up for it.      That sounds amazing. I’d love to go. Maybe I can go with you on the holiday if I get my license sorted.      You’d be a good travel companion, love. You always know how to make the most of a trip.      Well, I think we should start planning. I’ll talk to the insurance company this week and see what options we have.      That sounds great.

So, Dad, I’ve been trying to get my phone to stop buzzing so much with those Facebook notifications. I can’t even read a book without it going off like a party horn!      You think that’s bad? I used to get phone calls all the time from people who thought they were calling me on the landline. You know, before mobiles were everywhere. I still have that old rotary phone in the attic, but I’ve never dared to use it.      That’s the past, though. I mean, I’ve even tried to use the app, but it’s just too complicated. You know, like that one time when I tried to order groceries online and ended up buying a whole bag of glitter for the kids’ art class. I think the app thought I was an interior decorator.      You always had a talent for making mistakes in the most inconvenient ways. Remember when you thought the floor was a spare bedroom and tried to sleep on it? It took me three hours to get you out of there.      Oh, come on, that was only once! And I was just trying to work on my sleep habits. You know, like the old days when we could just lie in bed and watch the sunrise instead of scrolling through Instagram. It was peaceful, if you don’t count the constant arguing about what to have for breakfast.      Yeah, those were the days. Remember when we used to go to the market every Saturday and pick out fresh produce? Even back then, I had to remind you not to buy the same thing every time. You’d end up with ten bunches of bananas and no idea what to do with them.      Those were the days. But I think I’ve finally learned my lesson. I even signed up for a food bank delivery service. It’s not the same as picking out fresh vegetables, but at least I don’t have to worry about running out of food.      That’s good. You’re smart, you know. I still can’t wrap my head around the idea of food banks. I remember when life was simple—just a bit of bread, some tea, and a few biscuits. And the weather was always better than it is now.      Yeah, I miss those days, too. But I think I’ve got it figured out now.

So, I was just telling my mate about that time I tried to play golf for the first time. I thought it was just swinging a club and hitting a ball. I ended up looking like a confused raccoon trying to hit a moving target.      Oh man, I can relate. I tried playing golf with my dad last year. He was like, “You’ve got the natural talent of a man with a golf club.” I just stood there hitting the ball into the bush like it was a bad habit.      You’re not the only one. I remember when I tried to learn how to use sarcasm properly. I thought it was just saying the opposite of what you mean. Then I turned to my best friend and said, “Oh, I think I’ve got a new nickname for you.” And he goes, “Blimey, you’re a real comedian.”      Yeah, I once tried to be sarcastic in front of my sister and completely messed it up. She looked at me like I’d just said the word “plastic” in a funeral. I was like, “Hey, isn’t that a really cool way to say ‘I’m not impressed’?”      That’s the thing about sarcasm—it’s like a language all its own. I remember my gran once told me that my last name, “Williams,” was originally a nickname for someone who was really good at winning arguments. You know, “Williams” means “one who wins.”      Oh, that’s a good one. I heard that my surname, “Johnson,” actually comes from the old English word for “master of the house.” So I guess I’m the master of my own home, even though I’m still trying to figure out how to fix the toilet.      At least you know where you came from. I have no idea where my family name comes from, but I’ve got a feeling it’s something like “Harrison,” which I think means “someone who’s always on time.” But I’m always late.      That’s the thing about surnames. They’re like a mystery waiting to be solved. I tried to research mine last year, and it turns out my ancestors worked in the textile industry. That explains a lot.      So, does that mean I’m a descendant of kings? I mean, my surname is “King.” You know what that means, right? It’s like, “You’re the ruler of everything.”

So, what’s the deal with you lot? You’re always out having fun while I’m stuck in this flat with a ceiling that creaks like a haunted house.      Hey, you got a flat? I thought you were still in that dodgy shared house with the roommate who thinks they’re a professional wrestler.      Yeah, but I’m finally moving out. Found a place in Doncaster. It’s got a garden and a proper fridge. I’m not gonna chase a diet of takeaway and squashed meat anymore.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? You know, I’ve been trying to eat more vegetables and less takeaway. But when you work in manufacturing, you’re always too tired to cook.      Yeah, I get it. I’m working shifts in Cambridge, which means I’m either at the site or asleep. No time for meal planning.      I know what you mean. I’m a production controller, so I’m always on call. But I’ve started taking lunch breaks to walk around the local park. It’s a little thing, but it helps.      That’s actually a good idea. I’ve been trying to do more exercise, but I’m always too busy with event planning and deadlines.      Event planning? You’re not even in a rush, are you? I’m out there getting my hands dirty, lifting bricks and digging ditches.      I know, I know. But you can’t blame the job for being a bit… gritty. Maybe I should start going to the gym more. I’ve got a gym membership, but I just keep forgetting.      I’ve been there. I’ve got a gym pass too, but I’ve only used it once. You need someone to drag you there, honestly.      Maybe we should all do something together. Like, grab a drink, then go for a run or something.      That sounds like a plan. I could do with some fresh air.      I’d like that. It’s funny how we all have different lifestyles but end up talking about the same things—work, food, and how to stay healthy.      To health, then. And to not being so stuck in our own routines.      To not being stuck.      And to not living in a haunted flat.      Cheers, then. Alright, what are we doing this weekend?      I’m thinking of going to that pub in Ely. They’ve got a good live music scene.

Well, I've just been on a call with my niece. She was talking about the eclipse. She said it was absolutely incredible—like the sky turned black and the stars came out like crazy. I told her I wish I could have seen it, but I’ve been stuck indoors with the weather being so awful.      Aye, I know what you mean. I tried to get out with the binoculars but it was so cloudy. I’ve heard the eclipse was a big deal, but I’ve been feeling pretty low lately. You know, with the TV licence and all. I don’t even know why we still have to pay that. It’s been a community hub for years.      Yeah, I saw that too. It’s ridiculous. I mean, the library isn’t just a place to borrow books—it's where people come together. But honestly, I think the best way is to start with the people who live and work in the area. We can’t rely on outsiders. The more local support we have, the better. I mean, the library’s been part of this neighborhood for decades.      You're right. And we need to be proactive. There’s also this thing about the borough council considering changes to work shifts. I’ve noticed more people are complaining about the hours. It’s like they’re trying to make it harder for people to access services.      I’ve heard that too.
