That sounds like a good move. I’ve been considering something similar. I left my school job last year to start my own tutoring business. It’s not as stable, but I love the independence.      That’s brave of you. I admire your courage. I’ve always wanted to do something like that, but I’m not sure I have the confidence. What’s your experience like so far?      It’s been a rollercoaster, honestly. Some days are great, and others are exhausting. But I’ve made some great connections and even started working with a few local schools. Oh, and I’ve been experimenting with some new beauty products. I’ve been into natural skincare lately.      Oh, I’ve heard about those. I’m always looking for something that doesn’t irritate my skin. Do you have a favorite brand?      I swear by a brand called  The Ordinary . It’s affordable and effective. I’ve even started making my own face masks with ingredients I can buy at the local market. It’s fun and a bit of a creative outlet.      That sounds amazing. Maybe I should try that. I’ve always been into DIY stuff. Speaking of which, how’s your dog doing? I heard you got a new one last year.      Oh, he’s a good boy. His name’s Max. He’s a rescue dog, a mix of a German Shepherd and a Border Collie. He’s a handful, but he’s the best companion I could ever ask for.      That’s lovely. I have a cat named Luna. She’s a bit aloof, but she’s adorable. I think she’s planning to take over the house.      She sounds like a bit of a diva. But I can’t imagine life without Max. He’s my constant companion.

So, I've been meaning to ask, what's the deal with this whole Passover Seder thing? I mean, I know it's about the Exodus and all, but I've never really gotten into the whole ritual. Do we even have to do all those things?      Oh, you're gonna  love  it, really. It's like a family story-telling event with a ton of food and tradition. The Seder plate has all these symbolic foods—like the bitter herbs, the matzah, and the wine. It's all about remembering how the Israelites left Egypt in a hurry, right?      Exactly, and the whole night is structured around the Haggadah, which is the story of the Exodus. It's not just about the past; it's about passing down the narrative through generations. I find it deeply moving, especially when the kids are involved. It's like a living history lesson.      I get the cultural part, but what about the food? I mean, I know people like to eat matzah and bitter herbs, but are there any other dishes we have to make or eat?      Oh, there are so many! The main thing is that everything has to be kosher. So no meat and dairy together, and everything has to be prepared according to strict dietary laws. We usually make some of our own recipes, like karpas, which is a green vegetable dipped in saltwater, and charoset, which is like a sort of sweet mixture made from fruits and nuts.      Wait, charoset? That sounds like something I could make at home. I’ve seen it in some restaurants. I think it’s like a fruit spread?      It’s definitely more of a textured paste. It’s supposed to represent the mortar the Israelites used to build bricks, so it’s kind of a symbolic food. But it’s also delicious. I remember my mum used to make it with apples, cinnamon, and walnuts. It was always a hit at the Seder.      Speaking of food, I’ve been meaning to ask—what happened with the Ortolan you mentioned earlier? I’ve heard it’s a rare bird, and it’s supposed to be a delicacy in some parts of Europe.      Oh, that’s a big one. It’s a type of thrush that’s only available in certain areas, like France. They’re usually served in Parisian restaurants, and it’s a very exclusive dish.

So, I just finished this amazing book about the history of knitting. It was so fascinating how it evolved from a necessity to an art form. I’m thinking of starting a small knitting group in the community center.      That sounds like a great idea! I love how crafts can bring people together. But wait, haven’t you already started your own knitting project? I saw your scarf on the couch last week.      Oh, that’s just a started project. I’ve been struggling with the pattern. I keep making mistakes, and it’s so frustrating. I thought I’d like to teach it to others so I can practice with them.      If you want, I could help. I’ve been knitting for a while now. So, I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen the new episode of  Mindhunter ? I think it's the one where they're digging into the murder cases from the 70s again. Anyway, I’ve been meaning to get a Kindle because I’m about to run out of paperbacks. I’ve been reading a lot of mystery novels lately, and the Kindle makes it easy to carry around a whole library. Well, I've been thinking, lass, about how we're all just sitting here doing nothing. It's not like we're young anymore, and yet we still have time on our hands. So, I've got this idea for the party. We could have a themed night, like 'Take Me to the River' or something. I mean, it's not too complicated, and it might be fun for everyone. Hey, have you heard about the new project at school? I’m so stressed about it. The teacher said we have to do this giant presentation on climate change, and it’s due next week. We’re in this together, so let’s make it work.

So, did you actually get through to the restaurant, or are we still just winging it? I’d rather not end up at some random place because we got mixed up with the reservations. You've been co-ordinating projects all week, and you haven't even managed to get your turkey sandwich from the café. Besides, you need to eat. You're not the only one who's been working hard.      That’s true, Mummy. I know, I know. I just feel like I’ve been in a loop of meetings, emails, and spreadsheets all week. I barely have time to stop and think, let alone eat. That sounds perfect. I’m just hoping I can keep up with the conversation. My brain is already on autopilot.      You’ll be fine. You just need to take a deep breath and enjoy it. Not if I get to you first.      Alright, alright. Let’s just enjoy the meal and let the stories come later.

So, I've been meaning to ask you, how's everything going with your kids? I know they're both in high school now, and I’m always curious about their lives.      Oh, they’re alright, you know. Right, so I’ve been thinking about this new shift I’ve got at the bar. It’s not bad, but I’m not sure I can keep doing it for much longer. Yeah, I’ve got a sixth form diploma, and I’m still just working as a barista – no one’s got a chance, really. It’s a bit of a catch-22. I suppose that’s the reality of being a student. You’re just trying to make ends meet. I’ve got a couple of exams coming up, and I’m not sure how I’ll manage the workload and the job at the same time. It’s a bit of a balancing act.      It really is. I can only imagine how tough it must be for you. But I have to say, I admire how you’re managing it.

So, I've been meaning to ask, what are you all planning for your holidays? I know it’s got to be a bit of a blur with the library schedule, but I've got a bit of time to myself. Can you believe the way they played that last goal? I mean, they had like three players in the box and no one touched the ball. I don’t even know how they scored!      Yeah, it was a bit of a mess. But I guess that’s what happens when the manager doesn’t have a plan. I mean, we all know they’re not the best team, but you’d think they’d at least stick to a strategy.      I don’t know, maybe they’re just waiting for the right moment. You know, like,  this  goal was a complete fluke, right?      Oh, I’m not sure. Oh, come on, they’re not that bad! They beat us last month, remember? I still can’t get over how they managed to take the lead in the 89th minute.      Yeah, and we were all like, “Oh no, here we go again.” But at least they’re still in the race. I mean, the way things are going, they might even finish in the top half.      Who knows? I think the only thing that matters is the food. I mean, I’m not even sure why we’re watching this. I’d rather be eating something decent.      Yeah, I know. I’m just trying to pass the time. You know, maybe we should order some fast food.      Actually, that sounds good. I was just thinking about it. Do you want something specific?      I think I’ll go for the chicken burger. But only if you promise not to eat the fries.      Deal. But only if you promise not to eat the chicken.      You’re not serious, are you? That’s the best part of the meal.      Yeah, I guess so. But I think I’ll save the fries for later. Maybe we can have a proper meal sometime soon.      Yeah, I’d like that. But for now, let’s just focus on the game and the food.

You know, Mum, I still remember watching  Doctor Who  on a rainy afternoon in Manchester when I was a kid. It was the old days, before everything went digital. So, I’ve been thinking about Pancake Day this weekend. I’ve got a plan to make a huge stack of pancakes, like the ones we used to have when we were kids. Hey, did you guys get the takeaway? I ordered it ten minutes ago, and it’s still not here. I’m starving.      Don’t worry, I called the restaurant and they said they’re running late. They said it should be another 15 minutes.      I don’t think they’re running late—they’re just lazy. Not like some sort of mystery meat that’s been sitting in a box for days.      I get what you’re saying. I once had this chicken dish that arrived so late, I ended up eating it for dinner and then again for breakfast. It was like breakfast, but with more sauce.      That sounds like a disaster. So, I was just thinking about the old days, you know, before all this driverless car nonsense. It was so much more fun back then, wasn’t it? I remember when we’d all pile into the car, and we’d argue about who got to sit in the front. It was chaos, but it was  fun .      Oh, I remember that well. Your mother used to take us all to the seaside every summer. I still remember the smell of the sea air and the taste of saltwater on our lips. But what about the rice krispy cakes? You used to have to wait until you got home to eat them, didn’t you?      Yes! My uncle used to say they were a reward for good behavior. I think he made up the rules, though. He did have a way with words, didn’t he? I mean, he was a teacher, so he had that kind of charm. I wonder how he’d react to all this new technology now. You know, the driverless cars, the smart homes, even the way we shop online. It’s all so different from when he was growing up.      I think he’d be amazed. He always said he’d never live to see the day when we wouldn’t have to do the grocery shopping ourselves. But then again, he was a meticulous man. He even kept a ledger for every single expense.      Yeah, and he was always telling us about the old days when he was an accountant. He used to say that the only time he felt really safe was when he was in those old offices, with all the paper and the typewriters.

Okay, so I was thinking about Chinese New Year, and I wanted to show the kids how to draw a dragon. I remember when I was a kid, my mum used to do that every year. Thanks! I also want to try drum lessons. I heard it’s like playing with your hands and feet.      That’s a fitting analogy. You’ll have so much fun with all these hobbies. Speaking of which, have you ever tried Chinese food?

So, what do you think of Rome so far? I mean, it’s like... every cliché you’ve ever heard about Europe, right? Ancient ruins, tourists everywhere, and the weather is like a sauna.      Yeah, it’s been a bit too hot for my taste. I didn’t expect the heat to be this intense. But I’ve been enjoying the food. The pasta here is incredible. Actually, I had this amazing carbonara at that little place near the Colosseum.      That’s the thing about Rome—it’s so full of character. You can’t help but feel like you’re stepping into a movie. Speaking of which, I’m thinking of starting a café here. I’ve got this little space on Via del Corso. It’s tiny, but it has a great view of the piazza.      That sounds cool. You ever think about how it would work? I mean, running a café in Rome? I guess it’s like any other city, but maybe the competition is fierce?      It’s not that bad. People love good coffee and a friendly atmosphere. Plus, I’ve already got some local connections. My brother’s been helping me out with the permits.      That’s awesome. You know, I’m actually looking to move to Italy. I’ve been in Rome for a few months now, working as a barista at this little café near the Pantheon. It’s not the most glamorous, but I love being part of the community here.      Wait, you’re Australian? I didn’t expect that. I thought you were more of a Londoner.      I grew up in Melbourne, but I’ve always wanted to live somewhere different. Rome has been a dream for me. Plus, the pace is slower, and I like the way people here talk. It’s not like back home.      You know, I think I’ve heard your accent before. You sound like you’ve got that mix of Australian and English. Is that from growing up in a multicultural family or something?      Yeah, my parents were both immigrants. My dad from England, my mom from Syria. I grew up speaking English and Arabic at home. So yeah, I guess that’s where the mix comes from.      It’s interesting how accents can tell a story. I think that’s what I love about meeting people here. Every conversation is a little different, whether it’s from London, Birmingham, or even from overseas.

So, I've been meaning to ask you, how do you find living in Holsworthy? I know it's a bit of a change from Southend, but I hear it's a lovely place to settle down. So, I've been thinking about getting a new laptop. My old one's starting to crash every time I try to stream some cricket or something. It's getting on my nerves, you know? So, I've been thinking about the heating in this place. I know it's old, but I’d like to get it fixed properly before the weather turns. I just finished my meal, and I can't stop thinking about that paper I had to read this morning. It was about the psychological effects of long-term remote work on mental health. Honestly, it felt like a bit of a downer, but I guess it's all part of the job. I can relate. I had to attend a meeting this morning about our new assessment tools for students. I even had a conversation with my colleague the other day about how mental health is often overlooked in the academic world, especially for postdocs. That's so true. I remember when I first started, I didn’t take the stress as seriously. I thought I was invincible. But then, a couple of months ago, I had a breakdown. It was scary, but it taught me a lot. I started taking more time for myself, even if it’s just a walk or a cup of tea. I admire that. I’ve been trying to do the same. I've taken up running again, which helps clear my mind. It’s not that I’m perfect, but I’m at least making an effort. I think it's important to set boundaries, even if it’s just for yourself. Exactly. And you know what else? I think they're starting to understand that it's not just about ‘being strong’. That's great to hear. I've been trying to encourage my parents too, but it's not always easy. I think when you’re older, you're more used to certain ways of doing things. But I've noticed that a lot of my friends in our age group are really open about mental health now. I couldn’t agree more. It's a shame that it took so long for people to open up about it, but I think we're in a better place now.

So, I was just telling my wife about the time I tried to cook a roast dinner and ended up setting the kitchen on fire. It was a complete disaster, but we all laughed about it afterwards.      I remember when I tried to make a soufflé for my mum’s birthday. It was supposed to be a surprise, but it collapsed like a pancake. I had to explain it was just a “new recipe.”      My sister tried to make a soufflé once, and it ended up in the bin. She said it was a “delicious mess.” I still don’t know if she was being sarcastic or not.      I’ve tried cooking more than once, but I always end up burning something. The only thing I can cook is toast, and even that sometimes turns out breakfast.      I’m not cooking anything, thanks. I’m too scared of the kitchen. My mum used to say I was born with a knife in my hand, but I think she just wanted an excuse to make me do dishes.      Tell me about your family, Speaker_3. You said you’re from Ashford. Any interesting tales from growing up there?      Oh, there’s so many. My cousin once tried to teach the family dog to do tricks. He got it to roll over, but then it started barking at everything. We thought it was hilarious at first, but it got annoying.      I had a cat when I was a kid, and it used to knock over everything. My mum would say it was “the devil incarnate.” I used to love watching it chase that ball of string.      My dog’s got the same habit. It’s like it’s trying to break the house. I’ve tried training it, but all it does is run around in circles.      I have a cat, but it’s the opposite. It’s very lazy. It sleeps all the time. I think it’s got a secret life.      Lazy is better than chaotic, I think. I’d rather have a calm cat than a hyper dog.      To animals, then. May they all live long and be happy.      To animals. And to not burning down the house again.      And to not setting our kitchens on fire.      And to not getting stuck with the dishes.      And to not being left-handed. I tried to hide it for years, but it’s just part of me.

So, I've been meaning to ask—what's with the name  ANON ANON ? It’s like a username or something. I’m not sure if it’s a joke or just a placeholder.      Oh, it’s a nickname we picked when we first started hanging out. It’s a play on the word “anonymous,” but we thought it was funny because we were all kind of hiding from our real lives. Or at least, pretending to.      Honestly, I think it was more about the vibe. We were all in the middle of some weird phase—like, trying to make it look like we weren’t trying too hard. But now that we’re out here on holiday, I’m starting to think it’s not so much about hiding anymore.      Yeah, but I still don’t get the  ANON  part. It’s like, are we actually anonymous? Like, no one knows who we are? I mean, we’re all British, right? I don’t think we’re actually that secretive.      It’s more of a code name for our group. Like, if someone were to ask about us, we’d just say “ANON ANON.” It’s kind of got a sarcastic edge to it. Plus, it makes us sound like we’re part of some secret club.      I think it was meant to be a bit of a rebellion. We all felt like we were stuck in our routines back home. So, we decided to give ourselves a new identity—like, we were going to be anonymous for a while. It was a way to break free, even if just for a little bit.      It’s kind of fitting, actually. We’re all kind of stuck in this loop of work and life. I mean, I run a café,  Speaker_1  is a student,  Speaker_2  works at a bakery, and  Speaker_4  is a barista. It’s like we’re all just trying to make ends meet and stay afloat.      And yet here we are, having lunch in a restaurant that’s completely empty. I mean, it’s the kind of place you’d see on a documentary about food tourism. But still, it’s weird to be in a restaurant by ourselves.      Exactly! It’s like we’re the only people here. I wonder if it’s because of the time of day or maybe the location. This place is in East London, so maybe it’s not the kind of area that gets busy at lunchtime.

So, I'm telling you, I've been swiping left and right on Tinder for weeks and I've only had one guy message me back. I got that too. Like, what does it even mean to “play it safe” with the drinks? Are we literally just supposed to not drink at all? Or is it like, you  don't  get drunk and then make a mess?      My friend, you’re living in a fantasy land. That guy just wants to see if you’re a risk-taker. I mean, the only thing he’s actually offering is a date, not even a conversation. Well, I've been thinking about the new benefit changes they've announced. It's all a bit of a mess, isn't it? I mean, how are we supposed to plan for the future if the rules keep changing? You know how they talk about "job readiness" and "supporting the workforce"? It sounds like they just want to keep people down. I built bridges and roads, and now I’m just sitting here, trying to figure out how to survive.      It’s not just you, mate. I’ve seen the same thing. I know how hard it is, especially for someone who’s always been independent. I used to run a childminding business, and I was always on my feet. Now I just sit here, waiting for the next letter. It’s exhausting.      I've been watching a lot of TV lately. I’ve been catching up on some old dramas, but I’m not really into the new stuff. It’s all too fast-paced and full of special effects. I find it hard to connect with anything these days.

So, did you manage to get the grant application in before the deadline? I saw the email from the council this morning.      God, I was so close. So, I've been thinking about the weather again. It’s been so damp in Tarnow lately, isn’t it? I mean, I’m used to Cambridge, where it’s either sunshine or a flood, but this is like a soggy blanket wrapped around you all day.      Yeah, I know what you mean. It’s been miserable. Oh, and I was just scrolling through my social media and saw this photo of my sister from last summer, laughing with my parents at the family holiday. It made me feel so homesick.      I totally get that. It’s strange, isn’t it? I went back to England for my uncle’s funeral last month, and even though I was sad, I felt like I was back in the place where I belong. But when I come back here, I feel like I’m in a completely different world.      It’s weird, isn’t it? I feel the same way. I do miss the way people talk in England—there’s something about the rhythm of it. I’ve tried to keep up with the dialect here, but it’s just not the same.      I know. I can imagine. I’ve always loved teaching, but lately, I’ve been feeling like I need to take a break. I’ve been thinking about going back to England for a while. It’s tough, isn’t it? But I think it’s okay to not have all the answers. I just hope I can figure it out before it’s too late.      I hope so too.

You know, I’ve been thinking about my job lately. The copywriting gig has been pretty hectic. I’ve been up until 2 a.m. a few times, and I’m starting to feel like I’m not even being paid properly for the hours I put in.      I get that. I’ve had a few of those moments too. It’s better to have this part-time gig so I can keep studying and not feel like I’m wasting my time.      Yeah, I guess that’s a good point. I’ve been telling myself that if I can just find a better job, I’ll be able to step back and take a breath. But it’s so hard to find something that pays well and gives you creative freedom.      It’s tough, isn’t it? I mean, I’m in a better position financially than you are, but I’m not exactly living the dream either. I’m still paying off my student loans and trying to save for the future.      I can relate. My parents always said I should have been a teacher or something stable, but I just love writing. I mean, I was lucky enough to get a graduate degree, which is a bit of a luxury. But even then, I’m still doing what I always did: writing for people who don’t even know me.      That’s a bit sad, isn’t it? I go to university, get a degree, and then end up programming surveys for people who barely know what they’re doing. But maybe that’s just life.

Okay, I've got to get up early tomorrow for that Neon Moon event. I was woken up by the roosters at about 5:30 this morning. I've been trying to get some rest, but it's impossible.      Yuck, roosters? That’s so annoying. I didn’t even know they were still around here. I thought they were a thing of the past.      They’re everywhere! I tried to sleep last night, and one of them was right outside my window. It was like a soundtrack to my nightmares.      I know, I tried to sleep too, but I kept thinking about the circus skills workshop I’m doing tomorrow. I’m so excited. It’s supposed to be a hands-on experience, learning juggling and balancing.      That sounds fun! I wish I could go. Mom says I can come if I help her in the kitchen this morning. She’s making pancakes, and I’m kind of good at flipping them.      I can help too! I’ve been practicing my pancake flips in the bath. I got it down to three seconds.      Oh, really? That’s impressive. I’m not sure about the pancake flipping, but I do know how to juggle. I learned it during my postgrad studies. It’s actually a great stress reliever.      Wait, you can juggle? That’s so cool! I wish I could do that. I tried once, and I dropped a ball on my foot. It hurt!      That’s not so bad. I dropped a marble on my toe once, and it was worse. I had to walk around the house for an hour with a bandage on.      You two are such drama queens. Anyway, I’m thinking about the Neon Moon event. It’s a community gathering, and there are some Australian phrases being used. I remember hearing them at the market last week.      Like what?      Things like “barbecue” and “arvo.” I think it’s a way to make the event feel more colorful. The organizers said it’s a celebration of culture and community.      Do you think they’ll have a circus tent? I really want to see the performances.      Yeah, I think there will be a few different acts. I heard they’re doing fire dancing and acrobatics. I’m really looking forward to it.      I hope we all get to go. It’s going to be so much fun!      I’ll bring my lucky hat.

So, I just read this article about the new election promises. I’m trying to figure out if it’s worth voting for any of them. You know, with all the wars and inflation, it’s hard to see how anyone can fix things.      I know, it’s a mess. But I think the real issue is how the government handles the economy. If they can’t get inflation under control, nothing else matters. I’ve been reading about this new policy on tax cuts for small businesses. It’s supposed to stimulate growth, but honestly, I don’t see how it’s going to help the average person.      Yeah, I’ve heard about that too. But I still can’t get over how the previous government just kept raising taxes without fixing the actual problems. I mean, I’m a student, but even I feel the pressure. My parents are struggling to make ends meet, and I’m not even working yet.      That’s a shame. I remember when I was your age, we had more stability. My dad was a teacher, and he always said that education was the key to a better life. But now, I don’t know if that’s true anymore. I’ve seen too many people fall through the gaps.      I was just thinking about that. My grandfather was a miner in Wales, and he always spoke about how hard life was. He told me stories about how they used to have a better system—stronger unions, more support for workers. Now, it feels like everything’s been privatized. You can’t even rely on the NHS anymore without waiting months for appointments.      It’s not just the NHS. I’ve been trying to apply for a grant for my university project, but the process is so slow. I’m starting to wonder if I should even bother. I mean, if I can’t even get the support I need to finish my degree, what’s the point?      That’s a real problem. I know it’s a tough time, but I still believe in the system. You just have to keep pushing, even when it feels like no one’s listening. I remember when I was editing books, I used to do the same thing. Every time I faced a block, I’d just keep going, and somehow it always worked out.      I respect that.

Okay, so I was thinking about our stories again, and I had this idea for a new chapter. It’s set in a quiet village, like Comberton, actually. I was wondering if you two would like to help me flesh it out.      That sounds exciting! I love stories, especially when they’re based on real places. I just got back from the Linton Book Festival, and I heard Helen Moss talk about her village inspirations. She said she uses her hometown as a character in her books. Maybe we could do something like that?      Yeah, I like that idea! My dad used to tell me stories about Bury St Edmunds when I was little. He said it’s like a character itself—full of secrets and old buildings. Maybe we could make the village in our story feel like a living thing?      That’s a great point. I was thinking of making the village a bit mysterious, like in Helen Moss’s work. There could be a hidden part of the town that only a few people know about. It would be a great place for a secret or a mystery to unfold.      I love mysteries! And I think it could tie in with the Linton Book Festival. Maybe our characters could go to the festival and discover something about the village’s history, like Helen Moss did. It would be fun to have some connections to real events or places.      You know, I saw a poster for the festival at the library last week. They had a special session with Helen Moss where she talks about how she blends real and imagined elements in her stories. Maybe we could include something like that in our story—like a character who gets inspired by the festival and starts writing their own book.      That’s a brilliant idea. I was also thinking about the language. Since we’re all from different parts of England—Dartford, Norwich, Bury St Edmunds—maybe we could include a bit of regional dialect in the story. It would make it feel more authentic.      I like that. I’ve heard different accents and ways of speaking in the South of England. Maybe we could let the characters speak in a way that reflects their background. It would make the story more vivid.      I think it would help readers feel more connected to the characters. Plus, it might even make them want to visit the places we’re talking about.

Okay, I’m just trying to figure out what’s in this packet of spices. Is it for the lentil curry or the chilli? I swear I labeled them both, but now I can’t remember which is which.      Oh, that’s the one with the cardamom. You’re making the lentil curry again. It’s like your signature dish now. I’ve started thinking you should open a restaurant.      Honestly, I’m not sure if I’d trust you with a restaurant. You’ve been known to accidentally set the oven on fire twice. But the curry? That’s another story. It’s practically  shmeat  compared to the real thing.      Thanks, I’ll take that as a compliment. Speaking of  shmeat , I was reading this article last night about how lab-grown meat is becoming more accessible. It’s like the future of food. No animals involved, no environmental damage. Just... science.      I’m not sure I’m ready for that. There’s something about cooking with real ingredients—especially when it comes to meat. But I do get the environmental angle. I mean, cows produce a lot of methane.      Yeah, plus the ethical side. I’ve seen the videos of factory farms. It’s not just about the environment, it’s about exploitation. But then again, I’ve been in abattoirs too. It’s not perfect, but at least the animals are treated better than in some places.      I guess it all depends on your values. I’ve been thinking about going fully vegetarian for a while now. It’s not just about the animals—it’s about the planet, too. I mean, I take vitamin tablets every day to make up for the lack of B12. It’s not fun, but it’s worth it.      I’ve been there, too. I took a break from meat after watching that documentary about animal cruelty. But I still feel like I’m being too strict. I don’t want to miss out on the taste of a good steak, even if it’s from a sustainable source.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? The line between ethical eating and indulgence is blurry. I’ve even started drawing some comics about it. It’s kind of like  Curb Your Enthusiasm —you think you know what you’re doing, but your ego gets in the way.      Oh, I’ve seen your comics!

So, I was sorting through the kitchen cupboard the other day, and I found this old jar of pickled onions from the 70s. I mean, they were  still  edible, but I don’t know, it felt like throwing away a piece of history.      I can relate. I tried to get rid of all the old pots and pans last week, but my wife said it was like throwing out a memory. She even mentioned my dad’s old teapot—still works, by the way.      That’s so weird. I just got rid of my old toy collection last month. I was stressed about space, and I realized I hadn’t played with most of them in years. But I kept the ones from my childhood, like that little plastic dinosaur.      You’re lucky you still have that. My mum still has her old washing machine from the 80s, and she insists it’s the only one that doesn’t leak. It’s got more stains than the walls of my flat.      I remember when we got our first washing machine. It was like a big event. My mum even got a new dress for the occasion. But now I’m not sure if it’s worth it. I mean, I’m not even sure if it can handle a load of laundry anymore.      Did you ever think about upgrading? I read that a new washing machine can save a ton on energy bills. But I guess it’s not the same as having something that’s  been through it all .      Exactly. I think it’s more about sentiment than function. My sister even said she’s going to throw out her old wedding dress next year. She’s getting a new one for the anniversary.      That’s a bold move. My wife insisted on keeping hers, even though it’s practically a museum piece. She said it’s  her  story.      You know, I took the plunge and got a new washing machine last year. It’s the quietest thing I’ve ever owned. But I still miss the sound of the old one. It was like a reminder that we were all still in the same place.      There’s something about the old things, isn’t there? They make you think about where you’ve been and where you’re going.      Maybe that’s why we hold onto them. Even if they’re broken, they remind us of who we used to be.

Okay, so I just got this weird request from a colleague. They want me to explain what a  butterfly fork  is. I’ve never heard of it before. I mean, I know there are different types of forks—like the dinner fork, salad fork, fish fork—but a butterfly fork? Has anyone ever used that?      Wait, isn’t that the one with the little tongs on the side? I think my nan used to have one. She used it for serving desserts or something. But I never saw her use it at the table. Maybe it’s more of a decorative piece?      Yeah, I think it’s the one that looks like a butterfly because of the tongs. I remember seeing it in a museum once. But I don’t think it’s common in modern households. Why would someone want to use it now?      It’s part of a set of cutlery that goes back to the Victorian era. I think the idea was that it could be used for both eating and serving. But I’m not sure why it’s called a butterfly fork. Maybe because of the shape of the tongs?      Wait, my dad once told me that in the 19th century, people used these forks to serve food at the table, especially for fancy occasions. It was a sign of status. But now it’s just a novelty item. Maybe it’s what the colleague is referring to.      I think the colleague is also talking about a  two-minute silence  for a friend’s birthday. I mean, is that a thing? Like, being quiet for two minutes to make a toast or something? I’ve heard of people doing quiet moments for memorials, but not sure about birthdays.      Oh, it’s a trend! I read about it a few weeks back. It’s a way to show respect and reflection, even on a birthday. It’s supposed to be a moment of silence where people don’t speak or make noise. It’s a little surreal, but I think it’s becoming popular. Though I’m not sure if it’s widely accepted.      I think it’s part of a wider movement around mindfulness and celebrating life. Maybe the colleague wants to do it for their partner’s birthday. They mentioned it in passing at supper. I’m trying to figure out the best way to explain it to everyone.

Okay, so I was thinking about our holiday plans for next year. I’d love to take the kids to Cornwall again. I heard there’s a new attraction there that’s really popular with families.      Cornwall? That sounds like a great idea! I remember last time we went there, we had so much fun at Porthcoven beach. Mom said we could go back next year if we wanted.      I loved the beach! I got to build the biggest sandcastle ever. But was it the same one as last time, Mom?      Yes, it was. But I think there’s something new near there now. You know that Adventure Island series? There’s a new one opening in Truro, and I think it’s part of the V&A exhibition tour. I think it’s going to be an adventure for the whole family.      Adventure Island? That sounds exciting! I’ve heard about it. I think it’s supposed to be based on the books, right?      Exactly! I’ve been reading up on it. Wait, did they say it’s for kids? I don’t want to be bored, Mom.      No, no, it’s for all ages. I think the theme park is specifically designed to have different zones for various age groups. And also, I’ve got exam marking this week, so we’ll have to plan this around my schedule.

So, I just got a text from my mum saying that the roads are really bad near Sunderland. She’s got to go to a meeting in Newcastle today, and she’s worried about the traffic. So, I just got an email from the Chinese restaurant down the street saying they’re running out of the Peking duck and the Shanghai noodles. I was really hoping to get those. Maybe they’ve got something from the northern or southern parts of China? I remember hearing that some of the chefs there specialize in different regional styles.      Yeah, I think they mentioned having some hot pot options, but I’m not sure if that’s a good idea. I’ve only had it once and it got too spicy for me.      Well, maybe you could go for the chicken in black bean sauce. I think that’s always a safe bet. It’s got a nice balance of flavors, and it’s not too heavy.      Or maybe you could go for the beef with broccoli? I’ve had that before, and it was really good. I think it’s a bit more of a classic dish.      Hmm, I like the idea of the beef with broccoli. It’s not too complicated and it’s something I can eat without worrying about the spice level. But I’m not sure if they still have that.      Let me check my phone. So, I've been meaning to ask you, how do you feel about the NHS these days? I know it's been a bit of a hot topic lately. So, I heard the council’s been cracking down on immigrant landlords again. You know, they’re shutting down places where people are renting out rooms without proper licenses. I retired a few years back, and now I just live off my pension. But even that’s not safe. I’ve seen friends get taken advantage of by bailiffs, and it’s heartbreaking.      It’s got to stop, you know? There’s a huge divide between people who are working and those who aren’t. You know what I found interesting? I read an article about the police being involved in some of these cases. They’re not just enforcing the law—they’re doing it in a way that targets people who are already vulnerable.      Aye, and it’s not just about welfare. It’s about control. I’ve heard the police take on an almost militaristic role now. That’s the thing, though. Everyone’s waiting for the next shoe to drop. I had a friend who was a young mum, and she got a job in the service sector. She was working 60 hours a week, but then she got told she was no longer eligible for benefits. It was like a gut punch.      Yup, and that’s the crux of it. People are working harder than ever, but the system is designed to keep them down.

Okay, I think I’ve found that report we were supposed to review. It’s got some interesting data on vowel shifts in northern English dialects.      Yeah, I remember you mentioning something about regional phonetic changes. But honestly, I’m still not sure if we’re seeing real linguistic drift or just a lot of social influence.      That’s the debate we’ve had for months. It’s like trying to figure out if people are changing their speech for the sake of being trendy or because of real language evolution.      I think it's a bit of both. But what’s really interesting is how these shifts are being documented in academic circles. I mean, I’ve seen some pretty comprehensive studies on this.      Wait, you’re saying that dialects are actually changing? I thought they were more static. I mean, I grew up in Leeds and I still speak the way I did when I was a kid.      I think that’s a common misconception. Dialects do shift over time, especially in urban areas. My hometown in Sunderland is a good example. The vowel sounds are starting to get more like those in the south.      But that’s not just about pronunciation. It’s also about how people identify with their regional identity. If someone starts speaking more like the south, does that mean they’re losing their local identity or adapting to a broader cultural context?      That’s a key point. Identity and language are intertwined. I’ve seen research showing that language change can be a way for people to negotiate their place in society.      Exactly. And the more people are exposed to different dialects through media and education, the more likely they are to adopt certain patterns. It’s a complex interplay of social, cultural, and linguistic factors.      So, does that mean we’re heading toward a more homogenized language? Or is there still room for regional variation?      I think there’s definitely still room for variation. But I do wonder how much of that variation will survive in the next generation.      That’s the beauty of language, isn’t it? It evolves, adapts, and keeps changing. We just have to keep documenting it all.      And we’ll be here to do that. You know, I think we’ve done more research on language shifts than most of our colleagues.      It’s not just research—it’s part of who we are.

So, I've been thinking about this whole thing with the internet and how it's changing the way we communicate. You know, with all the social media and streaming services, it's like we're living in a global village now. But do you think it's actually making us more connected or just more isolated?      That's a good question. I reckon it depends on how you use it. Now, even if you don’t speak another language, you can still get by with Google Translate.      Exactly. I think part of it is the shift in how we perceive language. It’s no longer just about communicating—it's about understanding cultures, right? So if you can’t even understand the nuances of a language, how can you really grasp the culture behind it?      I couldn’t agree more. And that’s why I’m trying to learn Spanish this year. It’s not just for work—it’s about connecting with people from different backgrounds. I was in Madrid last summer, and the locals were so friendly, but I felt like I was missing out because I couldn’t really chat with them properly.      That’s a great point. I’ve been trying to learn some basic phrases too. I even signed up for a language exchange group. It’s like meeting people who are learning your language in return. It’s a win-win. Plus, it’s a great way to practice.      Sounds like a solid plan. I should really get myself into something like that. Maybe we could do a language swap sometime? I’ve got some Spanish, and you’ve got a bit of French, right?      Absolutely! We could meet up after work. Maybe at that café we always go to.

So, I was just telling my granddaughter about the time her nan tried to fix the plumbing in the old house in Hull. She thought she could do it with a spanner and a bit of grit. Turned out, she just clogged things up more.      Yeah, I remember that. You didn’t even let her use the spanner, did you? I think you just stood there and laughed as she got covered in sludge.      Oh, I tried to help, but I was just as clueless as her. I remember trying to open the valve and it just whistled like a banshee. I thought it was the ghost of the old house.      We had the same problem with the pipe in the old flat. I tried to unclog it with a wire, and it just made it worse. I ended up calling a plumber and spent more than I’d like to admit.      You were always the one who could tell the difference between a toaster and a breadmaker. You even tried to fix the fridge once and ended up with a whole mess of wires and a burnt-out fuse.      Mate, you got the same result. I remember you tried to fix the light switch and ended up with sparks flying like it was a fireworks show. You didn’t even know what a screwdriver was.      Oh, I know what a screwdriver is. I just had the wrong one. I think I used a knife instead. I thought it was a bit more romantic.      That’s the spirit. We were all trying to be handy, even if we ended up making things worse. I remember the time we tried to fix the roof. You thought you could just nail it down with a few boards. The wind came in and the whole thing collapsed. We were all under it, laughing and shouting.      Yeah, and we had to wait two days for the roofer to come. I remember the look on your face when you saw the damage. You looked like you’d been eaten by a wild animal.      I still have the photo of that. It’s a family treasure. You were all covered in dust and leaves, and you were smiling like you’d won the lottery.      I still talk about that every time I see a roof. I remember thinking I was the first person to ever build a house without using a single tool.

So, I just got these photos from last summer in Kyoto. I was so excited to take them, but honestly, I’m not sure if I’m proud of them or not. You were a bit nervous at first, but once you got into the rhythm, you started capturing some really nice moments. That shot of the cherry blossoms by the river— that  one was brilliant. You really got the light just right.      Oh, you saw that? I was so nervous about that one. I kept waiting for the perfect moment, and when it came, I didn’t even realize I was taking the photo. But then I saw it on my phone, and I thought, “Wow, that actually worked.” It’s funny how sometimes the best shots are the ones you didn’t plan for.      Exactly. And I think that’s why I love traveling with you—because you’re always looking for the little details. Like the way the light hits the streets in Tokyo, or the way the local markets are always so vibrant. I’ve always said that if you’re going to travel, you should go with someone who’s as curious as you are. You’ve always been the one to dig deeper, to ask questions, and to really connect with people.      I think that’s why we’ve always been such a good team. You push me to see the world differently, and I push you to see the beauty in the ordinary. I think that’s what makes our trips so special.      Yeah,

So, I just had the best night out last week, like, the kind of night where you think, “this is how it’s supposed to be.”      Oh, really? You’re suddenly the life of the party? That’s a big shift for you.      Yeah, I know, I’m not usually the one who’s out all night. But I met this guy at the bar, and he was so chill. We ended up going to this tiny music venue in Shoreditch. It was packed, but we got a booth near the stage.      Wow, that sounds amazing. Did you talk much?      We did! He’s into football, which I guess is a plus. I’m not super into it, but I tried to be friendly. We even ended up hanging out at his place after, just chilling and watching a film.      Whoa, did you even think about what you were doing? You’re not usually the type to go out like that.      I know, I know! But I’ve been feeling like I need to step out of my comfort zone. I mean, I still live with my parents, and I’m studying at university, but I feel like I’m stuck in this bubble.      That’s understandable. I’ve been trying to do the same thing. Last week, I went to this bar with my roommate, and we ended up at someone’s house. It was weird, but fun.      Yeah, I think we’re all just trying to find our way. Anyway, I brought a cat home with me that night. I was like, “Okay, I’m living the dream,” and then I had to take care of a cat.      Oh no, did you mean to bring it home?      No, it was passed around by my friends. They told me it was a “company cat,” and I thought it was a joke. But I ended up taking it to my place. Now I have to walk it every day.      That’s insane! But also kind of adorable. I’ve got this dog, and sometimes I wish I had a cat. They’re easier to take care of, I think.      I don’t know, I’m learning. Anyway, what’s your latest move?      I’m trying to go to more parties. I’m even thinking about joining a club or something. Maybe even try out for the sports team.      That’s so cool.

So, I've been meaning to ask you, have you got the arrangements for the grandmother’s visit sorted yet? She’s coming down from Belfast next week, and I’d like to make sure everything’s ready.      Actually, I’ve been thinking about that all week. I called the hotel in Hunsonby last night, and they’ve confirmed the booking for her. She’s staying in one of the family rooms, just like old times. Speaking of which, I overheard some folks at the café talking about the current FIFA rankings. Do you think England’s still in the running for the World Cup?      Well, I’d say yes. They’ve been doing well in recent tournaments. I remember when I was teaching, I used to follow the games closely. But enough about football—let’s get back to the grandmother. So, I've been trying to set up my Blackberry again, and it's been a nightmare. I got the voice recognition software installed, but it keeps mishearing me. I think it's because I've got a heavy accent or something. I mean, it's not like I'm trying to speak in a different dialect, I just say things the way I always have.      Oh, I remember when I first got one of these things. I tried using it to send a text, and it misread "I'm going to the shops" as "I'm going to the shops." Get it? It said "shops" like "shoos." It was so awkward. You know, like that one time when I accidentally sent a message to my ex saying I was "shooing" him, instead of "going" to the shops? That was an epic fail.      You know, when I was younger, I had one of these early smartphones, and I used to try and use the voice command. One time, I was trying to set a reminder for the grocery store and said, "Remind me to buy milk." It said, "Okay, I will remind you to buy milk." Then I asked, "What time?" I've been using an older model, and it's just not as smart as the new ones. I've had to set up my own reminders manually. But you know, I actually like that. There’s something nice about writing things down. It makes me feel more in control.      Yeah, but I thought voice recognition would make life easier. Especially with all the stuff I have to do with my flat. Like, I always lose my glasses. I was trying to find them the other day and said, "Hey, where are my glasses?" and it just ignored me. I almost lost my temper.      Oh, I've been there too. I tried to use the voice command to find my glasses once, and it said, "I can’t find that." I was so confused. I thought it was broken or something. You know, it’s like trying to teach a computer how to understand human emotions. It doesn’t get it.      I still think it’s amazing how much technology has advanced.

So, did you see the results for the match last night? I was watching it on my phone, and it was a huge upset. The local team won 2-1, and I just couldn’t believe it.      Yeah, I saw it too! I was in the café, and the barista was talking about it all day. It was like the whole place was buzzing. I’ve been feeling so homesick lately, especially with the weather being so gloomy. It’s like the autumn is just dragging on and on.      I know what you mean. I’ve been getting really bad with the SAD lately. I’ve been trying to get out more and do things like visit the park, but it’s just not the same. I think I’m going to try to get some light therapy.      That’s a good idea. I’ve heard it works really well. I mean, I’ve been in Poland for over a year now, and I miss the rhythm of life back home—like teaching, the students, even the long walks with my dog.      Oh, your dog! Did you mention to me that you’ve got a puppy now? I thought you were going to adopt a cat.      No, I actually got a golden retriever. His name is Max, and he’s the best. He’s always running around the apartment, and he’s even been helping me with my teaching. He sits quietly when I’m grading papers.      That’s adorable. I’d love a dog, but I don’t think I could handle the responsibility. I’ve been thinking about getting back into teaching, though. I used to do it part-time, and I miss the interaction with the students.      That sounds like a great plan. I know how passionate you are about language. I tell you, I feel responsible for my students all the time. They’re preparing for their exams, and I don’t want them to fail.      I can only imagine. I used to work with ESL students too. It was such a rewarding experience, even when things got tough.      Yeah, it really is. I think it’s why I’m still here. I’m trying to build a future, even if it’s a bit uncertain.      I admire that. You’ve got a lot of drive. I’m just trying to figure out what I want to do next.

So, I just got a text from my sister saying her new dress is so tight it’s making her feel like she’s got a corset on! I don’t know how she manages to walk in that thing.      Oh, I’ve seen that kind of thing before. My cousin got one like that for her birthday. She said it was “the ultimate statement piece” – but I think she just wanted to feel like she was being watched by everyone in the room.      Honestly, I’ve seen some of the most ridiculous outfits in my dating life. I once went out in a dress that only came up to my knees and had a built-in skirt that you couldn’t really see. I looked like I had two layers of fabric on, and I couldn’t even sit properly.      I can imagine. You always have to be careful when you’re dating – what’s appropriate for one person might not be for another. Speaking of dating, how’s your love life going, Speaker_2? You’ve been single for ages now.      Honestly, it’s been a bit of a struggle. I work long hours, and I don’t really know how to approach people in a way that’s not just awkward. I mean, I’m not the most social person, and I don’t know what to say when I’m out with friends.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I tried going out with someone who was into the arts, and it ended up being a disaster. We had so many different goals and about five different conversation topics that never aligned.      I think that’s part of the learning curve. I mean, it’s not like you’re supposed to be perfect at first. I’ve been dating someone for a while now – we met at a work event. It was awkward at first, but now we’re really starting to click.      How did you even start talking?      We were both trying to get a coffee, and we started talking about the goings-on at the office. It was weird at first, but then we just started clicking. I think it’s all about finding the right person who’s into the same things.      I think that’s the key. You don’t need to be perfect – just compatible. Speaking of compatible, have you ever thought about what you’d do if you got a promotion?      Honestly?

So, I've been thinking about our discussion last week about teaching English in China. I've been talking to a colleague who's been teaching there for three years now. He mentioned something about the difference between teaching in a city like Beijing versus a more rural area like Yunnan. He said it's quite a contrast—urban students are more tech-savvy, but the rural ones are more curious about Western culture.      That sounds interesting. It can be, especially if you don't have the right connections. You have to go through the proper channels, and sometimes the approval process is slow. But if you’re flexible and willing to adapt, it can work. I’ve heard some people who teach in Yunnan actually end up staying for years.      That’s quite a commitment. Though, honestly, the majority are just curious. I think the interest in Western culture is a big draw for many students.      That makes sense. I’ve also been curious about the education system in China. How does it compare to the UK? I mean, the language teaching methods must be quite different.      Absolutely. In China, they often focus more on grammar and structure, whereas in the UK, we encourage fluency and speaking ability. I’ve seen some programs that blend both approaches. I’ve been thinking about it myself, just not sure where to start.      I’ve thought about it too. If you wanted to, I could help you find some contacts in the field. There’s a group of ex-teachers who might be willing to mentor you. Plus, I’ve got a colleague who’s been teaching in Xi’an and would love to chat about the experience.

So, what’s the plan for tomorrow? I was just thinking, maybe we could go to that new café in Newcastle. I heard the coffee’s amazing.      Newcastle? You know I hate driving through that part of the city. I mean, I love the place, but the traffic? It’s like a war zone.      Yeah, I know. But it’s worth it for the coffee and the view of the Castle. Let’s make it a treat. I’ll even bring my own laptop so you don’t have to listen to me ramble about the coffee.      You’re on. But only if you promise not to talk about the coffee for the entire time. I swear, you could lecture me on the beans for an hour.      Deal. But what about the car? We’ll need to pick it up from the garage. I called them yesterday, and they said it’s ready by tomorrow morning.      Good. I’ll drive then. You’ve had enough of the seatbelts and the traffic. I’ll take you to the café, and then we can hit up a few spots downtown.      Wait, do you think we could do a bit of shopping after? I’ll pick you up at 10. We’ll grab breakfast on the way, and then we can start our day.      Sounds perfect. I’ll be ready. Hey, you've been really quiet lately. Everything okay? I noticed you've been working late a lot and haven't been hanging out with the group like usual.      Honestly, it's been… complicated.
