I’ve heard stories about people getting suspended for falling for a patient. It’s not something you take lightly.      I get it. But you’re not the only one who’s felt this way. I’ve had a few break-ups recently too. It’s like your heart just doesn’t know what to do. You’re so used to being in control, but when someone actually  gets  you… it’s overwhelming.      Yeah, I can relate. I had this guy at work too—he was always there for me, and I really looked up to him. We started hanging out, and for a while, it was amazing. But then it all went sideways. I feel like I’m stuck between two worlds—work and personal life.      You know what? Maybe that’s the point. Maybe it’s not about choosing one over the other. Maybe it’s about finding a balance. Or maybe it’s just time to take a step back and go out with the group again. You don’t have to do this alone.      Thanks, I really needed to hear that. I’m going to try. I mean, I can’t ignore the feelings, but I also can’t let them ruin everything.

Okay, so I was reading this old legend the other day about the Green Man, and it got me thinking—what do you two think about the idea that good and evil are more like two sides of the same coin?      Hmm, what’s a Green Man again? I’ve heard of the Green Man, but I’m not sure what it is exactly.      I think it’s like a mythical creature, right? Maybe a guardian of the forest or something?      Exactly! The Green Man is a symbol from ancient pagan times, often depicted with leaves and vines growing out of his face. People used to believe he protected the land, and that he was kind and wise. But then, over time, some people started to see him as more of a trickster or even a monster, depending on the story.      Wait, so is he like a good guy or a bad guy? Because sometimes stories change depending on who’s telling them.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? Stories can shift over time, and the way we see good and evil can change too. Sometimes what was once considered evil becomes a part of something beautiful, like a legend or a folktale. And vice versa.      Like the Little Red Riding Hood story? I mean, the wolf is evil, but sometimes people say the wolf just wanted to have a good time or was misunderstood.      Exactly! And that’s what makes stories so powerful. They let us explore different sides of human nature. Some people think the world is black and white, but I think it’s more like a spectrum. There’s always a bit of good in the bad, and a bit of bad in the good.      So, does that mean there’s no true evil? Or does it just depend on the perspective?      Good question. I think it depends on the context. If someone hurts others for no reason, that’s pretty clear-cut. But if someone makes a mistake out of ignorance or fear, maybe they’re not truly evil. They just need to be understood.      So, like if someone does something bad but then changes their ways?      Exactly! And that’s what makes stories so important—there’s always a chance for redemption. Even the darkest legends can end with a lesson or a moral. It’s about how we choose to see the world.

So, did you see the photos from the school filming trip? The kids were jumping around like they were in a movie. I swear, half of them had their faces painted like they were auditioning for a Marvel film.      Oh, I saw the one where the kids were pretending to be knights and there was this girl in a green cape who looked like she was about to levitate. I couldn’t stop laughing. It’s so cute how they’re so into it. I just wish I could be that enthusiastic about school trips again.      Mum, I was the one with the green cape! I told them I was a dragon, and the teacher said I could stay on set for the whole day. I got to hold a fake sword and run around pretending I was fighting the castle.      That’s the best! I was the knight with the helmet. I almost fell over when I tried to swing the sword, but I didn’t want to look silly. I think I got more attention than the real actors.      Wait, you were the knight? That’s incredible. I would have been too scared to try that. But seriously, I thought you were still in a cast from your leg. You okay?      Yeah, the leg’s been better. I can still run, just not jump as high. I promise I didn’t jump off anything. I just accidentally tripped on a piece of cardboard. It was kind of funny.      Did you fall? I thought you were doing a cannonball into the pool. I saw the teacher try to catch you and then you just  flopped  into the water.      Oh no, the pool scene was a mess. I thought it was going to be a documentary about the school, but the kids were too dramatic. I mean, they were  very  dramatic. I still haven’t stopped thinking about the one where they were trying to film a fight scene and everyone was yelling.      I think the kids are just trying to be cool. They’ve seen too many movies. I’m sure the teachers are just trying to keep them occupied. Speaking of which, did you hear about the gym? They’re getting new machines next week.      Yeah, I was thinking about going myself. I’ve been avoiding the gym for weeks. I’ve been told I need to start running again, but I’m scared I’ll fall over like those kids did at the pool.

So, John, I’ve been reading up on the Green Party again. They’re pushing real hard for more local initiatives and sustainable living. You know, more than just climate change, they’re into community projects and fair trade. Do you think they have a chance?      I’ve been thinking about that too, Roy. It’s one of those parties that’s growing in popularity, especially with younger folks. But I still think they’re too idealistic. They talk about changing the world, but how do you actually make policy work in the real world? Didn’t they get voted out in the last election?      True, but I think they’re gaining traction, especially in places like Brighton where people are more environmentally conscious. I met a few folks at the boot sale last weekend who were all into sustainability. One of them even started a community garden. It’s inspiring, isn’t it?      Yeah, I suppose. I did go to that boot sale, by the way. That’s where I picked up the old sofa we’re using in the shop. It was a real bargain—just a few quid. I mean, we’re not exactly in the luxury market, but we’ve got to make ends meet somehow.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? Running a small business, you’ve got to be creative. I’ve been thinking about starting a part-time course for older people. I’ve got a few ideas for weekend workshops—art, gardening, even music. It’s something I’d like to do, but I’m not sure how to go about it.      That’s a great idea, Roy. I’ve seen a few people about town who are looking for something to do. Maybe the local library could help out. I’ve been trying to get more people to use the community center, but it’s not easy to get them interested. You’d need to make it engaging.      I was thinking about it last night. I’ve got some connections with a few local artists and gardeners. We could partner up and offer something that’s both educational and fun. I’d need a little funding, though. Maybe the council would support it?      That’s the thing about small businesses—sometimes you have to be your own boss. But I respect your ambition. I’ve got a lot of respect for teachers, by the way.

So, I was at the supermarket the other day, and this guy came in with a massive container of pasties. He was like, “I’ve got a pasty for every day of the year!” I nearly fell over.      That’s the kind of thing that happens in the Midlands, I reckon. You know, where people have a strong connection with food, especially when it’s traditional. I mean, pasties are a big deal there, aren’t they?      Yeah, totally. But when I think about pasties, I can’t help but think of the  real  pasty, the ones from Cornwall or Devon. You know, the ones you can’t just get in a supermarket. They take hours to make, and the crust is like a pastry, not just a frozen block of dough.      Right, I remember when I was doing my PhD, I used to go to a place in Birmingham called The Pasty Place. They had the best ones. I mean, not bad, but nothing like the ones from the south-west. I’d say they’re more of a comfort food.      It’s funny how something so simple can mean so much to people. I remember when I was in Cambridge last year, I met a guy who was into plants. He had this whole thing about the  correct  way to water a succulent. He was like, “You don’t just spray it, you  submerge  it!”      That sounds oddly like a philosophy lesson. I’d say he was a bit of a plant guru. But I’ve got to say, there’s something about plants. They’re like a conversation you can have without talking. You just watch them grow.      Exactly. I think I’ve got a bit of a green thumb, actually. My flat has this little corner with a few herbs and some succulents. I’ve even started getting into hydroponics. I mean, I’m not going to grow a tree in a glass jar, but it’s a start.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? Even in a city like Cambridge, you can find a little bit of green. I mean, it’s not like we’re surrounded by fields, but you can still make a space. And it’s not just about plants—it’s about how you live your life. Like, even politics, finance, Trump, you can approach it like you’re tending to a garden.

So, I was just thinking about that episode of  Blue Peter  we watched last night. Remember when they showed off the killer whale? It was so impressive, wasn’t it? I mean, how do they even manage to train those animals?      Oh, I remember that. I think it was the one where they had the orca doing all those tricks. It was amazing how intelligent they are. I’ve always been fascinated by marine life. I mean, I’m not sure how you’d even begin to train a whale, but it’s got to be some kind of mind control.      Right, but it’s also so controversial. I heard some people are against it, arguing that it’s cruel. My colleague, Sarah, actually did a paper on the ethics of captive marine animals. She said that the stress levels in these animals are often high and that they’re not really being treated humanely.      Yeah, I agree. I mean, I love TV shows like  Blue Peter , but I can’t help but feel a bit conflicted. I mean, I grew up watching those shows—my parents used to love them. But now, with all the news about animal welfare, it’s hard not to think about what’s really going on behind the scenes.      Exactly. I remember talking to a friend of mine who worked on a documentary about sea lions. He said they were so wild and unpredictable, and even the trainers got scared sometimes. It made me think: is this really education, or is it just entertainment?      That’s a good point. And then there’s the whole issue of TV violence. I recently saw a documentary about how violent content affects kids. I was wondering—do you think shows like  Blue Peter  set a good example or maybe even encourage some of that behavior?      I don’t know. Maybe it’s the way they present things. Like, they show these animals doing amazing things, but they don’t talk about the real issues. It’s like they’re selling a product, not giving the full story.      Yeah, and then there’s the whole squatting thing. I’ve been reading about it in the news. Some people are squatting in old buildings in London, and the government is trying to get them out. It’s kind of like a modern form of protest, isn’t it?      I guess it is.

You know, I was talkin’ to the bloke from the hostel last week, and he was makin’ more sense than most of these folk I see round here. Seems like they’re all stuck in the same rut, frightened to take a step forward.      I know what you mean. I’ve been tryin’ to help a few of them with their forms, but they’re all so confused. It’s like they don’t know where to start. You’d think with the government bein’ so keen to help, things would be easier.      Oh, the government’s always talkin’ about helpin’ people, but when it comes down to it, they’re just throwin’ money at the problem. I’ve seen it in school, in engineering projects, in everything. It’s like they don’t really understand what people need.      Exactly! And the way they manage these hostels, you’d think they were run by the Ministry of Defence. It’s all red tape and no real direction. I’ve had to write letters and fill out forms for people who can’t even read them properly. It’s a real mess.      I remember when I was a childminder, I used to have to fill out forms too, but at least those were straightforward. Now, it’s like every service you need, you have to jump through more hoops than a politician in a speech. And don’t get me started on the language they use. Some of it’s like a foreign language to me.      I bet it is. I’ve been tryin’ to explain the difference between a science and an engineering degree to one of my students, and they thought they were the same thing. It’s like they’re all just tryin’ to get through life without understandin’ the basics.      You know, I was talkin’ to my brother yesterday about how hard our parents worked. They ran their shops, and they were always up at dawn, workin’ till late. They didn’t have the luxury of sittin’ around and complainin’.      Yeah, I remember my mum sayin’ that our family was like a little business. She’d go out every morning and come back with food for the whole week. It was like she was runnin’ an abattoir, but in a different way.      True. I think we’ve all got a bit of the hardworking gene in us. It’s just that nowadays, people are more inclined to sit and moan than get up and do somethin’.

So, I heard you were in recruitment before you became an associate lecturer. That must have been a different kind of work, right?      Oh, it was a few years ago, actually. I worked as a recruitment consultant for a bit, helping companies find the right people for roles. It was pretty intense, honestly. I used to meet with candidates all the time, run assessments, and basically act like a gatekeeper for some big firms.      That sounds like a lot of pressure. Did you ever find it frustrating? I mean, when you're in academia, the pressure is different—more about content and teaching rather than just selecting people.      Yeah, it was definitely a different kind of stress. In recruitment, you’re always trying to balance what the company needs with what the candidate is capable of. It’s not just about matching skills—it's about making sure the person is a good cultural fit too. But I guess that’s part of the job.      I can imagine. I remember when I first started teaching, I was nervous about how I was going to evaluate students’ work. I mean, I always thought of myself as a teacher, not an assessor.      It’s funny how the roles can shift. When I got into teaching, I had to start evaluating students’ assignments, and I had to get used to the idea that I was not just guiding them but also judging their work. It’s a bit of a shift, but I think it’s part of what makes the job challenging and rewarding.      I definitely agree. I had to evaluate a recent assignment from one of my students, and I found myself overthinking it. I kept wondering if I was being too strict or not strict enough. It’s hard to balance being fair with being encouraging.      That sounds familiar. I remember a student who was struggling with a particular assignment. I was tempted to give them a pass because they were putting in effort, but I also had to maintain standards. I had to remind myself that I wasn’t just a friend—I was there to help them grow.      Exactly. It’s a fine line, isn’t it? I think the key is to be clear with expectations but also empathetic. I’ve started using more formative feedback instead of just summative assessments. It seems to help the students understand where they need to improve.

Hey, you guys! I didn’t expect to see you all here. I mean, it’s like a mini reunion or something.      Oh, it’s not a reunion, it’s just me trying to find a book for my essay. But honestly, I haven’t been able to find the right one.      Same here. I’ve been trying to locate that book on postcolonial theory for ages. I swear, sometimes this library is like a maze.      I know, right? I literally just asked the librarian for help, and she said she’d be back in ten minutes. Now I’m stuck here, staring at this wall like it’s the Mona Lisa.      Well, I’m here to study for my exam. But I thought I’d come in early to get a good spot by the window. It’s such a nice day, and this place has the best light in the whole city, if I do say so myself.      Wait, you’re from Bradford? I thought you were from London.      No, I’m from Bradford, Yorkshire. Born and raised. I moved to Manchester for uni, but I still consider Bradford my hometown. It’s a bit of a culture shock sometimes, but I love it.      I’m from Bolton, Greater Manchester. So I guess we’re both from the North. It’s kind of funny that we’re all friends and yet we all come from different parts of the same region.      I’m from India. My parents moved here when I was a kid, so I grew up in Bolton as well. I speak English pretty well now, but sometimes I mix in a few words from Hindi.      Oh, that’s cool! I bet you’ve got some interesting stories about growing up here.      I do. Like the time I was trying to order a coffee and said, “Get me a cup of tea, please,” and the barista stared at me like I was speaking another language.      I’ve had that experience too. I once said, “I’ll have a small coffee,” and the barista looked at me like I was from Mars.      You guys are so funny. I think I’m going to start using some of these phrases in my essays.      You should! It adds flavor to your writing. And if you ever need help with your essay, just ask. I’m a student too, so I know how it feels.

So, I was just telling my cousin about the time I tried to join the military... got turned down because I had a bad cough. Absolute nonsense! I was fit as a flea, and they said I had a chronic respiratory issue.      That’s not the first time I’ve heard that. I have a cousin who tried to join the RAF, and they rejected him because he had a mild case of eczema. He said they were pickier than a barista about coffee grinding.      Sounds like they’re not just looking for healthy people—they’re looking for people who look healthy. I don’t know, maybe they’re just trying to keep the numbers low.      Maybe, but I still think the military is a good way to get structure and discipline. It’s not for everyone, but if you’re into it, it’s a solid plan. I’ve been thinking about applying for a part-time role in logistics, just to see what it’s like.      That’s a good idea. I’d say it’s worth it if you’re looking for steady work and a sense of purpose. But then again, I’ve always been more of a bookworm. I mean, I’ve got this pile of magazines I’ve been trying to read for months— National Geographic ,  Vogue , and  Tech Monthly .      You’re reading  Vogue ? I thought you were a conspiracy theorist. Wait, are you into the new film about the Space Shuttle? I saw the trailer and it looked wild.      Oh, I’ve been dying to see it. I’m the type of person who thinks space is the future, but I also need to be grounded. I mean, it’s a bit strange how we have spaceships but still can’t fix the Wi-Fi in our offices.      That’s the truth! I’ve been trying to get my boss to upgrade our IT system for months, and he keeps saying, “We’ll do it when we have the budget.” I’ve asked if we can work from home, and he said, “Only if you can find a good Wi-Fi signal.”      I think we need to rethink our approach. Maybe we should start a podcast about tech and space. We could call it  Beyond the Signal .      That’s a fantastic idea! We could get people like you, who actually know what you’re talking about, and me, who just loves complaining about the internet.

So, I just got back from the weekend trip to London. It was wild. I mean, it's always got that vibe, but this time was different. There were these two blokes from Manchester who came to visit, and they were complaining about the way people in London treat them. Like, they said they felt like second-class citizens everywhere we went.      Oh man, that’s not a surprise. I’ve heard that before. Some people in London, especially in the more trendy areas, act like they’re the only ones who matter. But then again, when you come from a place like Wirlpoole, you don’t  expect  to be treated like the local hero just for being there.      Exactly! I mean, I get it—London has its own culture, but it shouldn’t be used as an excuse to be rude. It’s like, if you’re not from there, you’re automatically an outsider. And honestly, I’ve seen that attitude from people from London too. They look down on people from the North.      Yeah, it’s so frustrating. I’ve heard stories about people in London being racist towards people from other parts of the country, even if they’re not from a different ethnicity. It’s like, if you’re from the North, you’re automatically assumed to be working-class, loud, or not educated.      That’s what I always say—people from the North don’t get the credit they deserve. I mean, I’m a film-maker, and my stories are about people from places like Wirlpoole. But when I go to London to pitch my work, people act like I don’t know what I’m talking about just because I’m not from there.      It’s so weird. My sister’s dating someone from London, and they’re like, “We’re not that different.” But they’re always making fun of the way people from the South speak. It’s like they think it’s a bad thing.      I think it’s a problem with the media too. All the ads and shows are always about Londoners. It’s like the whole country revolves around that one city. Even in architecture, where I work, the designs are all inspired by London. But I don’t know if that’s a good thing or not.      Honestly, I think we need to stop dividing ourselves like that.

So, you've just got here, right? How did the drive from Brighton go? I know it’s a bit of a long shot, but I’m sure it was worth it.      Oh, it was fine, thank you. We picked up some groceries along the way and stopped for a coffee in Lewes. It was actually really nice—very quiet on the road. Though I must say, the flat feels like a million miles away from the city.      Ah, yes, the flat. I remember when you first moved in, the place was just a shell. Now it's practically a  home . Still, I must say, I don’t think I've ever seen so many plastic bags in one place. You left them all out on the front step like they were a decoration.      Bingo! I was about to say something. You know, I’ve been working as a care assistant for years, and I’ve never seen such an accumulation of shopping bags in one place. I mean, why not just throw them in the bin?      Well, I’m not sure about the bins. I’ve been trying to get rid of them, but they keep coming. I guess it’s a habit. You know, I remember when we first got the flat, we were so excited about the kitchen. And now, it’s the heart of the house.      I know, right? I love how we’ve turned it into a cozy space. But I have to say, I still can’t get used to the way you pronounce  scones . It’s like you’re  sconing  them.      Oh, that's just the way we do it in the south. You know, you've got to make it sound like it's a  grown-up  treat. But I suppose it's all in the way you serve it—cream tea with a side of  diverticulitis  and a dash of cholesterol.      Oh, come on, that’s not fair. I've been with this flat for two years now, and I’ve never had a problem with  diverticulitis . I mean, I’ve eaten more nuts than most people, but I’m still here.      Well, maybe it’s the nuts that keep you healthy. Speaking of which, I’ve been thinking about taking a bike trip across the country. I heard the countryside is lovely this time of year.      That sounds amazing. But you’ll have to borrow my bike.

So, I just got this really weird message from my dad. He said he got a pop-up on his phone saying "You've won $500,000!" and he nearly fell out of his chair. I had to calm him down and remind him it's probably fake.      That sounds like a classic scam. I’ve seen those on Facebook before. They all have that same urgent tone. A lot of people fall for it because they’re hoping for something big, you know?      Yeah, and I think it's even worse when people don't know how to spot these things. My gran tried to send me a photo of the "win" once, thinking it was real. It took me a while to convince her it wasn’t genuine.      I know what you mean. I used to work in the civil engineering field, and we had a lot of people in our office who fell for similar scams. One guy actually sent money to a fake Nigerian prince account. Talk about a disaster.      Wow, that’s intense. I mean, it’s not like we’re in a place where people can afford to lose a few hundred pounds. I’ve been thinking about getting a better antivirus and maybe a firewall for my laptop. It’s got to be worth it, right?      Totally. I’ve been trying to set up a home office because of the remote work thing. It’s been a bit of a nightmare with the Wi-Fi and all. I think the house prices here in Cambridge have gone up a lot lately. I can’t afford to move, though, not with the cost of living being what it is.      Yeah, it’s about time people started taking housing seriously. I mean, the prices are just out of control. My friend Sam tried to buy a place last year, and it took him months just to get the mortgage approved. And he’s still waiting for the right property.      I know. I used to think I could afford to buy a place, but now I’m not so sure. It’s like the whole market’s just out of reach. I’ve been cooking more at home lately. It’s cheaper, and I think I’m getting better at it.      I’ve been experimenting with healthy recipes too. I’m trying to cut down on takeaway.

You know, I’ve been thinking about the new regulations at the hospital. It’s got me so stressed out. I was supposed to be on leave this week, but they’ve called me back in for extra shifts. I don’t know what’s going on.      That sounds rough. I was just at the clinic this morning, and the manager was talking about how they’re under so much pressure. I think it’s because of the new staffing guidelines. But honestly, do they even have the resources to handle this?      I totally agree. My boss at the care home keeps saying they’re “streamlining” things, but it’s just more work for everyone. I’m starting to think they’re not really caring about the staff. You know, I had to stay late last night to finish up an emergency shift, and I’m still exhausted.      I can only imagine. I was at the day center today, and the team was all so short-handed. One of the clients had a bad reaction to medication, and we had to call the doctor in a hurry. It was so stressful. I just wish we had more support.      Yeah, I’ve been there. I remember one time when I was working the night shift, and there was a patient who was in a lot of pain. I stayed with them for hours, and I didn’t even get a break. It was heartbreaking. But I guess that’s the price of the job, right?      It really is. I mean, we all chose this line of work because we care, but sometimes I feel like we’re not being treated like the professionals we are. I’ve been thinking about switching to a different field, you know? Maybe something more stable.      I’ve considered that too. I’m just worried about what else I’d do. I don’t know if I have the skills for anything else. But I do miss the days when I had more time with my family. Between work and my son’s school plays, I’m constantly running.      I know what you mean. My roommate is always reminding me that I need to take better care of myself. I’ve been trying to go to the gym more, but it’s hard when I’m so tired after work. Still, I think it’s important to find those little bits of time for yourself.
